senses.definition: Lose force or severity, or reduce the force of something; said of storms, pain, noise or strong feelings.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To die down or grow weaker, like a storm that slowly calms.

examples.text: The ferries stayed in port until the storm abated the next morning.
Her fear began to abate once the plane leveled off and the shaking stopped.
The city built sound walls along the highway to abate the traffic noise for nearby homes.
Public anger did not abate even after the mayor apologized, and protests went on for weeks.

distractors.lemma: Help or urge someone to carry out a crime or other wrong.
Give up a throne, or walk away from a duty one should carry out.
Make someone, often oneself, seem lower or less worthy of respect.
Damage a surface by scraping or rubbing it, as sandpaper does.
Officially cancel a law, treaty or agreement.

mnemonics: Abate comes from Old French abatre, to beat down: when a storm abates, its force is beaten down.

senses.definition: Markedly different from an accepted norm.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Different from what is ordinary, expected, or accepted as normal.

examples.text: The lab technician noted an aberrant cell structure that did not match the control sample.
Such reckless conduct was regarded as entirely aberrant for a diplomat with her record.
The algorithm flags aberrant spending patterns to protect consumers from fraudulent charges.
Doctors grew concerned when the scan showed an aberrant heartbeat, quite unlike the patient's usual steady rhythm.

distractors.lemma: So hateful that it fills people with disgust.
Complete and utter, used to stress how bad someone or something is.
Easy to see or work out without needing proof.
Rough enough to scrape or wear down a surface.
Present in large amounts, more than enough.

mnemonics: The word aberrant contains err, reminding you of behavior that errs from the standard path.

senses.definition: Slip away in secret, often taking money or goods that belong to others, to avoid being caught.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To run off in secret, often with stolen money, so you will not get caught.

examples.text: The corrupt treasurer planned to abscond with the charity's reserve funds before the audit.
Before the police could serve the warrant, the suspect managed to abscond across the border.
The accountant absconded with the cash from the safe and was never seen in town again.
Two prisoners absconded from the work camp during the night, and guards found their beds empty at dawn.

distractors.lemma: Soak up a liquid, as a sponge does.
Clear someone of blame or forgive their wrongdoing.
Go up, as a climber or an elevator does.
Be found everywhere in great numbers, as fish are in a healthy river.
Choose to go without something one enjoys, such as food or drink.

mnemonics: Abscond comes from Latin abscondere, to hide away: someone who absconds slips off and hides, often with the money.

senses.definition: Hold back by choice from doing or having something, especially a pleasure such as alcohol or rich food.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To choose not to do or have something you might enjoy, like drinking.

examples.text: My uncle has abstained from alcohol for twenty years and drinks only water or tea at parties.
Many Catholics abstain from eating meat on Fridays during Lent.
Runners are often told to abstain from sugary snacks in the weeks before a big race.
She decided to abstain from social media for a month and found that she slept much better.

distractors.lemma: Reach a goal or level after a long effort.
Keep hold of something rather than losing or giving it up.
Keep an effort or process going over a long stretch of time.
Have a connection with or bear on a certain subject.
Come to have something, often by asking or working for it.

senses.definition: Cast no ballot on either side of a question when a vote is taken.

mnemonics: Abstain comes from Latin abs-, away, and tenere, to hold: to abstain is to hold yourself away from something.

senses.definition: Speak to someone seriously about a fault or mistake, as a warning not to repeat it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To warn or scold someone in a serious but calm way.

examples.text: The librarian admonished the teenagers for talking loudly in the quiet reading room.
The judge admonished the lawyer for interrupting the witness and said a second outburst would bring a fine.
My grandmother would gently admonish us whenever we forgot to thank the cook.
After the referee admonished him for a rough tackle, the player kept his temper for the rest of the match.

distractors.lemma: Amaze someone so much that they can hardly believe what happened.
Tear down a building or other structure so that nothing usable is left.
Restore a supply to its full level after some has been used.
Get rid of a law, custom or system completely, so it no longer exists.
Hold someone or something dear and treat them with loving care.

senses.definition: Urge someone earnestly to do or avoid something, as a caution.

mnemonics: Admonish shares a Latin root with monitor: monere, to warn. To admonish someone is to warn them about their conduct.

senses.definition: Lower the quality of a substance by secretly mixing in something cheaper, weaker or harmful.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To spoil food, drink or medicine by mixing in something cheaper or harmful.

examples.text: Unscrupulous merchants would frequently adulterate olive oil with cheaper vegetable oils.
Testing laboratories check whether milk suppliers adulterate their batches with water.
The restaurant was fined after inspectors found it had adulterated its honey with cheap sugar syrup.
Dealers often adulterate street drugs with look-alike powders, which makes each dose dangerously unpredictable.
Laws exist to punish companies that adulterate food products for higher profits.

distractors.lemma: Heap flattery on someone, fawning over them like a devoted servant.
Give a rough outline of something without the details.
Wipe something out so completely that no trace remains.
Find words that express an idea clearly and in a sensible order.
Act as judge in a dispute or contest and make the official decision.

mnemonics: Adulterate comes from Latin adulterare, to corrupt, a close relative of adultery: both spoil something that should stay pure.

senses.definition: Relating to beauty, or to the way people judge and enjoy it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Having to do with beauty and how good something looks.

examples.text: The architects argued that the bridge needed aesthetic appeal as well as strength.
For purely aesthetic reasons, she painted the old radiator the same color as the wall.
The museum's new wing was a practical success but an aesthetic disappointment.

distractors.lemma: Practicing strict self-denial and avoiding comfort and pleasure.
Feeling no interest and making no effort.
Causing a loss of feeling or awareness.
Made in a factory from chemicals instead of grown or found in nature.
So weak or sad that it makes people feel sorry for it.

senses.definition: Pleasing in appearance; tasteful.

mnemonics: Aesthetic comes from the Greek aisthesis, "perception": it is about how things look and feel to the senses.

senses.definition: Raise the power or standing of a person or group, or make them look more important than they are.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To make someone more powerful or important, or to make them seem that way.

examples.text: The dictator used state newspapers to aggrandize himself, printing his portrait on every front page.
Rather than aggrandize his own role, the coach gave the players full credit for the championship.
The ambitious duke married his daughters into royal families to aggrandize his house and widen its lands.
Her memoir tends to aggrandize her part in the company's early success while barely mentioning her cofounders.

distractors.lemma: Add to the harm of something already bad, such as an injury or a quarrel.
Gather separate items into one mass or total.
Worry and struggle painfully over a decision.
Stir up public opinion by protesting or arguing hard for a change.
Treat someone unfairly so that they feel wronged.

mnemonics: Aggrandize contains grand, from Latin grandis, large: to aggrandize someone is to make them grander in power or in show.

senses.definition: The quality of responding quickly and gladly, without any sign of reluctance.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Being quick and happy to do something as soon as you are asked.

examples.text: When the boss offered him a paid week off, he accepted with alacrity.
The young apprentice tackled even the dullest chores with surprising alacrity, never needing to be asked twice.
Guests answered the invitation with such alacrity that every seat was taken within an hour.
The dog bounded to the door with alacrity the moment its owner picked up the leash.

distractors.lemma: Clearness of thought or expression, so that a point is easily grasped.
Loud laughter and amusement at something very funny.
Bold daring that ignores risk or good manners.
Stubborn determination to keep going and not let go.
A shockingly cruel act, especially one carried out in war.

mnemonics: Alacrity comes from Latin alacer, lively and eager, the same root as allegro, the music term for a quick, bright pace.

senses.definition: Lessen pain, distress or a problem so that a person can cope with it more easily, even if it does not go away.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To make pain, worry or a problem less bad.

examples.text: The new bypass should alleviate traffic on Main Street, though it will not end rush-hour jams entirely.
An ice pack helped alleviate the swelling in her ankle until she could see a doctor.
Food banks alleviate hunger in the city, but they cannot fix the low wages behind it.
Talking through the plan with his team did a lot to alleviate his worry about the launch.

distractors.lemma: Lift something up so that it sits higher than before.
Write a word or phrase in a shorter form, for example by using only its first letters.
Decide how much of a budget, time or space each person or task will get.
Turn a friend or supporter cold and unfriendly toward you.
Accuse someone of wrongdoing before any proof has been shown.

mnemonics: Alleviate comes from the Latin levis, meaning light, as in levity: to alleviate a pain is to make it lighter to carry.

senses.definition: Join two or more separate things, such as companies, groups or metals, so that they form a single body.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To merge separate groups or things into one.

examples.text: The two struggling school districts voted to amalgamate, forming one larger district with a single board.
Her novel amalgamates folk tales from three countries into one continuous story.
When the villages were amalgamated into a single town, residents argued over which name to keep.
For over a century, dentists have filled teeth with a paste made by amalgamating mercury with silver and tin.

distractors.lemma: Act to improve conditions that are hard or harmful.
Come out of a source and spread into the space around it, as steam does from a kettle.
Copy someone you admire in the hope of becoming as good as they are.
Fill something with life and energy.
Remove a limb by surgery, often after an injury or infection.

mnemonics: Amalgamate comes from amalgam, the blend of mercury and other metals long used to fill teeth: to amalgamate is to blend things into one.

senses.definition: Unclear in meaning because it can reasonably be taken in more than one way.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Could mean two or more things, so it is hard to tell which one is meant.

examples.text: The contract's ambiguous wording let each company claim that the other had broken it.
Asked whether he would run again, the senator gave an ambiguous answer that could be taken as yes or no.
The sign's ambiguous arrow pointed between two roads, and half the drivers took the wrong one.
Her text, 'Fine, do what you want,' was so ambiguous that he could not tell whether she was angry.

distractors.lemma: Having mixed feelings, drawn toward something and put off by it at once.
Eager to get ahead and willing to work hard for success.
Able to write, throw or work as well with one hand as with the other.
Suited to both land and water, as frogs and some military vehicles are.
Present all around in the surroundings, like background music or room temperature.
Lying right next to another area, with no gap between them.

senses.definition: Uncertain in nature or standing, and so hard to classify or judge.

mnemonics: Ambiguous begins with the Latin ambi-, meaning both: an ambiguous remark can be taken both ways.

senses.definition: Pulled between opposite feelings about the same person or thing, such as attraction and dislike.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Having mixed feelings, partly for something and partly against it.

examples.text: She felt ambivalent about the promotion: she wanted the higher salary but dreaded moving away from her friends.
Many residents are ambivalent about the new stadium, welcoming the jobs it brings but not the traffic.
He has an ambivalent relationship with his hometown, which he both misses and avoids visiting.
The review was ambivalent, praising the actors while calling the plot a mess.

distractors.lemma: Kind and generous, wanting good things for other people.
Wanting bad things to happen to other people.
Common at a certain time or place, found nearly everywhere you look.
Worth the same as, or doing the same job as, something else.
Showing great courage, especially in the face of danger.

mnemonics: Ambivalent joins the Latin ambi-, 'both', with valere, 'to be strong': two opposite feelings pull with equal strength.

senses.definition: Improve conditions that are bad or hard to bear, such as poverty, illness or unrest.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To improve a bad situation or condition.

examples.text: The city planted shade trees along the bus routes to ameliorate the summer heat for people waiting outside.
A second clinic helped ameliorate the long waits that patients had complained about for years.
Nothing the landlord did could ameliorate the damp, cold conditions in the basement apartment.
Free school meals were introduced to ameliorate the effects of poverty on children's learning.

distractors.lemma: Merge several companies or groups into one larger organization.
Honor the memory of a person or event with a ceremony or monument.
Explain something further by adding more details to it.
Weigh a decision slowly and carefully, often by talking it over with others.
Pay back a loan bit by bit in regular payments over time.

mnemonics: Ameliorate contains the Latin melior, meaning better: to ameliorate a bad situation is to make it better.

senses.definition: Something located at a time when it could not have existed or occurred.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Something that appears in the wrong historical era.

examples.text: A smartphone appearing in a nineteenth-century period drama is a glaring anachronism.
Viewers quickly spotted the anachronism of a Roman soldier wearing a wristwatch in the battle scene.
The novel contains an anachronism: a character in 1910 watches television, which had not yet been invented.
Fact-checkers flagged an anachronism in the script, since the song the hero hums was written thirty years after the story takes place.

distractors.lemma: The political view that people should live without any state or ruling authority.
A brief, memorable saying that sums up a piece of wisdom about life.
Ongoing hostility between people or groups who work against each other.
A word made by shuffling the letters of another word, as silent is made from listen.
A very precise clock, of the kind sailors once used to find their position at sea.

senses.definition: A person, custom or object that seems out of date, as if left over from an earlier age.

mnemonics: Anachronism contains the Greek chronos, 'time', as in chronology: an anachronism is something placed in the wrong time.

senses.definition: Similar or equivalent in some respects though otherwise dissimilar.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Like something else in some ways, though different in others.

examples.text: The heart is analogous to a pump, since both push fluid through a network of pipes.
Learning to code is analogous in some ways to learning French: both need grammar, vocabulary and daily practice.
The lawyers searched for an analogous case from the past, one close enough to guide the judge.
The economist argued that the housing bubble was analogous to the tulip craze of the 1600s, though the details differed.

distractors.lemma: Out of line with the usual pattern, and so puzzling.
Having a name that is not known or not made public.
Running its own affairs without control from outside.
Agreed to by every person involved, with no one opposed.
Inclined to break problems into parts and reason through them step by step.

senses.definition: In biology, doing the same job but not sharing an evolutionary origin, like the wings of birds and insects.

mnemonics: Analogous shares a root with analogy: when two things are analogous, you can explain one by drawing an analogy to the other.

senses.definition: A thing or result that breaks an established pattern and so stands out as odd or hard to explain.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Something odd that does not fit the usual pattern.

examples.text: A sudden cold snap in July was an anomaly that puzzled local forecasters.
Auditors flagged one anomaly in the accounts: a large payment that matched no invoice.
The researchers ran the test again to see whether the strange reading was a real anomaly or a faulty sensor.
After eleven months of steady growth, the sharp drop in March looked like an anomaly rather than a trend.

distractors.lemma: The condition of keeping one's name hidden or unknown.
A comparison that makes an idea clearer by showing how it resembles something familiar.
The study of how the bodies of people, animals or plants are built.
Self-government, or the freedom to make one's own choices.
Lasting ill will between people who dislike each other.

senses.definition: In astronomy, the angle that measures how far a planet has traveled around its orbit from the point nearest the sun.

mnemonics: Anomaly comes from the Greek an- (not) and homalos (even or regular), meaning it does not follow the normal pattern.

senses.definition: A deep-rooted, lasting dislike of a person, group or thing.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A deep dislike of someone or something that makes you want to stay away.

examples.text: The neighbors' antipathy went back decades, to a quarrel over a fence that neither would forget.
Despite her antipathy toward long meetings, she sat through the three-hour budget review without complaint.
His antipathy to cats was so strong that he crossed the street to avoid one.
The general's open antipathy toward the press meant reporters were rarely allowed near the camp.

distractors.lemma: A lack of interest or concern, so that nothing seems worth caring about.
The claimed power to send or read thoughts directly, without words or signals.
Something completely contrary to another thing, as chaos is to order.
A medicine that cancels out the harm done by a poison.
The medical science of how diseases arise and what they do to the body.

senses.definition: The object of a feeling of intense aversion; something to be avoided.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A specific person or thing that is the target of intense hatred and must be avoided at all costs.

examples.text: Public speaking remained the ultimate antipathy for the otherwise confident young writer.
For the pacifist philosopher, militaristic nationalism was the chief antipathy of his career.
Broccoli was the culinary antipathy that lingered from his childhood days.
The corrupt official became the primary antipathy of the reformist political movement.
Cats were his greatest antipathy

distractors.lemma: The cherished goal toward which all personal ambitions are directed.
A revered mentor who provides guidance during difficult times.
The primary source of financial support for a charitable institution.
A sacred artifact preserved within a historical museum.

mnemonics: Antipathy joins the Greek anti, 'against', and pathos, 'feeling': a feeling set firmly against someone or something.

senses.definition: A state of indifference in which a person feels no urge to care, take interest or act.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Not caring about something, and so not bothering to do anything about it.

examples.text: Voter apathy was blamed for the low turnout, as fewer than one in five residents bothered to cast a ballot.
The coach was frustrated by the team's apathy; nobody seemed to care whether they won or lost.
After months of bad news, a kind of apathy set in, and she stopped even opening her bills.
The petition met with apathy, as most shoppers walked past without even glancing at it.

distractors.lemma: A firm dislike directed at a particular person or thing.
The shrinking and weakening of a muscle or organ, often from lack of use.
The highest or most successful point of something, such as a career.
The act of turning away from a faith or cause that one used to follow.
The power of a story, speech or scene to stir pity and sadness.

mnemonics: Apathy is the Greek a-, 'without', plus pathos, 'feeling': apathy is a state without feeling or interest.

senses.definition: Quiet the anger or demands of a person or group by giving them some or all of what they want.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To calm an angry person by giving in to what they want.

examples.text: The airline tried to appease the stranded passengers with meal vouchers and free hotel rooms.
Nothing the manager said could appease the furious customer whose order had been ruined.
Critics warned that giving in to the dictator's demands would not appease him but only make him bolder.
To appease her toddler during the long drive, she handed him a bag of crackers.

distractors.lemma: Inspect something and set a value on it, as an expert does with a house or a jewel.
Seize a suspect and take them into police custody.
Tell someone the latest news about a matter so that they are informed.
Attach extra material, such as a list or footnote, to the end of a document.
Ask a higher court to overturn a lower court's ruling.

senses.definition: Satisfy a hunger, thirst or craving, at least for a while.

mnemonics: Appease has peace inside it, from the Old French pais, 'peace': you appease an angry person to restore the peace.

senses.definition: Needing great and sustained effort of body or mind, so that it tires out whoever does it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Needing so much effort that it wears you out.

examples.text: After an arduous six-hour climb through deep snow, the hikers finally reached the summit hut.
Rebuilding the town after the flood was an arduous task that took volunteers most of a year.
She called the bar exam the most arduous test of her life, after months of daily study.
Translating the ancient poem was arduous work, since every line had to be checked against three dictionaries.

distractors.lemma: Full of strong, eager feeling, such as love or enthusiasm.
Dry because almost no rain falls there, like a desert.
Clever at getting what one wants, often by sly or crafty means.
Chosen on impulse, with no rule or good reason behind the choice.
Known or understood by only a small group with special knowledge.

mnemonics: Arduous comes from the Latin arduus, 'steep': an arduous task feels like a long climb up a steep hill.

senses.definition: Put a thought or feeling into clear, well-organized words.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To say clearly what you think or feel.

examples.text: She struggled to articulate why the plan worried her and could only say that something felt wrong.
In his first speech, the new mayor articulated a clear vision for safer streets and better parks.
A strong essay articulates one main argument and backs it up with evidence.
Therapy helped him articulate feelings he had kept to himself for years.

distractors.lemma: Wave the hands and arms about to add force to what one is saying.
Sign up and be formally admitted as a student at a university.
Settle a dispute between two sides by acting as a neutral judge.
Guess at possible causes or outcomes while the facts are still unknown.
Move around a closed loop or system, as blood does in the body.

senses.definition: Say each sound of a word carefully so that a listener can catch it.
Connect parts by a joint so that they can move.

mnemonics: Articulate comes from the Latin articulus, 'small joint': to articulate a thought is to lay it out in clear, separate parts, like the segments of a finger.

senses.definition: Practicing strict self-denial and giving up comfort and pleasure, often for religious reasons.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Living very simply and refusing comforts and pleasures on purpose.

examples.text: The monks kept an ascetic routine of fasting, prayer and long hours of silence.
Her apartment was almost ascetic, with one chair, one lamp and nothing on the walls.
He gave up his car and his phone in an ascetic attempt to simplify his life.

distractors.lemma: Relating to beauty or to the enjoyment of beautiful things.
Sour like vinegar, or containing it.
Free from germs that could cause infection.
Denying that any god exists.

mnemonics: Ascetic comes from the Greek askesis, "exercise": an ascetic trains the body to do without comforts.

senses.definition: Ease a painful or unwelcome feeling, such as guilt, fear or grief, so that it troubles someone less.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To ease a bad feeling, such as worry or guilt.

examples.text: The surgeon's calm, step-by-step explanation did much to assuage the parents' fears about the operation.
He sent flowers and a long apology, hoping to assuage his guilt over forgetting her birthday.
Nothing the coach said could assuage the team's disappointment after losing the final in overtime.
Years went by, but time did little to assuage her grief over the loss of her brother.

distractors.lemma: Talk someone out of a plan or course of action.
Attack someone fiercely, with blows or with harsh words.
Weigh up the value, quality or size of something.
Treat something as a fact before anyone has shown it to be one.
Test a metal or chemical to find out what it contains.

senses.definition: Satisfy a need of the body, such as thirst or hunger.
Cause to be more favorably inclined; gain the good will of.

mnemonics: Assuage goes back to Latin suavis, sweet, the root of suave: to assuage a bitter feeling is to sweeten it.

senses.definition: Daring enough to try something risky that most people would not attempt.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Very bold and ready to take big chances.

examples.text: The explorer devised an audacious plan to cross the Antarctic continent alone on foot.
In an audacious move, the tiny startup offered to buy the company that had once turned its founders away.
The thieves pulled off an audacious robbery in broad daylight, strolling out of the museum past two guards.
Down by a goal with seconds left, the striker tried an audacious shot from the halfway line.

distractors.lemma: Possible to hear, even if only faintly.
Suggesting that things will turn out well.
Driven by an endless craving to pile up wealth.
Showing deep wisdom and sound judgment.
Regularly dishonest, with a habit of saying what is false.

senses.definition: Unrestrained by convention or propriety.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Disrespectfully bold and showing no regard for normal rules or manners.

examples.text: The junior clerk made an audacious demand for an immediate partnership during his annual review.
Critics condemned the playwright for his audacious disregard of historical facts.
Such audacious behavior at a solemn state funeral shocked the assembled dignitaries.
An audacious trick to pull

distractors.lemma: Meticulously compliant with formal etiquette.
Carefully reasoned and grounded in verified evidence.
Quietly observant without offering personal opinions.
Deeply reverent toward traditional authority.
Overly cautious when making public statements.

mnemonics: Audacious comes from Latin audere, to dare (not audire, to hear): an audacious person dares to do what others will not.

senses.definition: Stripped down to what is needed, with nothing added for decoration or comfort.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Very plain and bare, with nothing extra for looks or comfort.

examples.text: The monks slept in an austere stone cell that held only a narrow bed and a wooden desk.
After years of clutter, she furnished her new flat in an austere style, with white walls, one sofa and no pictures.
The writer favored austere prose, with short sentences and almost no adjectives.
Next to the gilded palace, the government office looked austere, with bare floors and metal chairs.

distractors.lemma: Sharp and shrewd in judging people and situations.
Grand and dignified, deserving deep respect.
Hard to grasp because it deals with obscure or deep ideas.
Lying in or coming from the southern half of the world.

senses.definition: Of a stern or strict bearing or demeanor; forbidding in aspect.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Having a serious, cold, or intimidating look and personality.

examples.text: The headmaster maintained an austere posture that made students hesitant to approach him.
Despite her austere expression, the teacher was remarkably kind to struggling students.
The judge gazed down from the bench with an austere countenance.
His austere demeanor often masked a surprisingly warm sense of humor.
An austere expression

distractors.lemma: Joyful and lighthearted in social interactions.
Overly talkative and eager to please others.
Confused and uncertain about the correct course of action.
Physically weak and lacking in endurance.
Extremely flexible in negotiations and rules.

senses.definition: Practicing great self-denial.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Living a very strict lifestyle without luxuries or physical pleasures.

examples.text: The hermit led an austere existence in the mountains, eating only wild berries and roots.
During the fast, they maintained an austere routine of prayer and meditation.
The founder imposed austere rules on the members regarding food and sleep.
He chose an austere lifestyle to focus entirely on his philosophical studies.
A desert nomad's austere life

distractors.lemma: Indulgent in rich foods and expensive wines.
Focused entirely on accumulating material wealth.
Extremely lazy and opposed to any form of labor.
Characterized by chaotic and unplanned activities.
Obsessed with modern technology and gadgets.

mnemonics: Austere goes back to a Greek word for a dry, harsh taste; an austere room is dry in the same way, with nothing sweet or soft added.

senses.definition: Put forward something as a definite fact, speaking as one who has no doubt about it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To say that something is true and leave no room for doubt.

examples.text: Questioned again under oath, the witness continued to aver that she had seen the defendant at the station that night.
The press release went on to aver that no customer data had been stolen, though it offered no proof.
Supporters of the new bridge aver that it will halve commute times, but the engineers are less sure.
My grandmother would aver to anyone who asked that her chicken soup could cure any cold.

distractors.lemma: Head off a danger or disaster before it can happen.
Make use of something on offer, such as a chance or a service.
Strike back at someone on behalf of a person who was wronged.
Hold someone in the highest honor, almost as if they were sacred.
Cut something off, or cut it into separate parts.

senses.definition: In a legal case, formally state a fact that one offers to prove.

mnemonics: Aver comes from Latin verus, true, the root of verify and veracity: to aver something is to declare it true.

senses.definition: Repeated too often; overfamiliar through overuse.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Boring because everyone has heard or seen it many times before.

examples.text: The pop song relied on banal lyrics about heartbreak and summer nights that listeners had heard a thousand times.
His speech was a string of banal phrases like 'think outside the box' that left the audience yawning.
They exchanged banal pleasantries about the weather before starting the meeting.
The movie suffered from a banal plot that we had all seen a dozen times before.

distractors.lemma: Willing to take bribes or do wrong for money.
Showing hostility in a way that hints at harm to come, like a cold glare.
Having to do with punishment under the law.
Having to do with the kidneys.

mnemonics: Something banal has been heard so often that you feel like putting a ban on all of it.

senses.definition: Cover up the true nature of something with an outward appearance that suggests otherwise.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To make something seem different from how it really is.

examples.text: Her cheerful smile belied the deep anxiety she felt about the exam results.
The shabby exterior of the restaurant belies the elegant dining room inside.
His soft, gentle voice belied a fierce determination at the negotiating table.
The calm surface of the river belies the strong currents that run underneath.

distractors.lemma: Talk about someone or their work as if it hardly matters.
Go over a point again and again, far longer than needed.
Grieve aloud over a loss or misfortune.
Beg someone earnestly for help or mercy.
Arrange in a will for someone to receive money or possessions after one's death.

senses.definition: Show that a claim or expectation was mistaken.

mnemonics: Belie contains lie, and comes from an old English word for deceiving: a calm face that belies your nerves tells a lie about how you feel.

senses.definition: Active in helping others, often through generous gifts or kind deeds.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Kind and generous, doing good things to help other people.

examples.text: The town still honors the beneficent mill owner who paid for its library, its school and its first hospital.
Each winter the beneficent couple quietly covered the heating bills of their elderly neighbors.
Far from being a cruel ruler, the old king was remembered as beneficent, lowering taxes and feeding the poor in lean years.
The charity's beneficent work, from free clinics to school meals, has reached thousands of families.

distractors.lemma: Splendid and grand, impressive to look at.
Lacking something needed, or too small in amount.
Getting tasks done fast and cheaply, with nothing wasted.
Living in ignorance, without knowledge or understanding.

senses.definition: Having a helpful effect, as good weather does on a harvest.

mnemonics: Bene means well and -ficent comes from facere (to do), so a beneficent act is literally doing good.

senses.definition: Make something such as an argument, a mood or an economy stronger by adding support to it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To give something extra support so that it becomes stronger.

examples.text: The government introduced new fiscal policies to bolster the sagging economy.
She used historical evidence to bolster her argument during the debate.
Engineers added steel beams to bolster the old bridge before heavy trucks were allowed to cross it.
Regular practice will help to bolster your confidence before the performance.
A surprise win in the first game did a lot to bolster the team's shaky morale.

distractors.lemma: Blow hard and noisily in sudden gusts, as a storm wind does.
Dash away suddenly, as a startled horse does.
Form small swellings filled with fluid, as skin does after a burn.
Shut someone away from the world, as in a monastery or convent.
Become infected and fill with pus, as an untreated wound does.

senses.definition: Prop a person up in bed with pillows or cushions.
Fill out or line something with soft padding.

mnemonics: Just as a bolster pillow props up your back, to bolster someone's case is to support and strengthen it.

senses.definition: Padded with grand, showy wording that hides how little is actually being said.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Using big, fancy words to seem important.

examples.text: The politician delivered a bombastic speech that lacked any concrete policy proposals.
Critics dismissed the novel as bombastic, full of grand speeches about destiny and very little story.
Stripped of bombastic phrases like 'a new dawn for humanity', the company's announcement was just a minor software update.
She preferred plain, direct prose to the bombastic style of some romantic poets.

distractors.lemma: Having to do with the flight of bullets, rockets and other objects that are fired or thrown.
Having to do with monks and their secluded religious life.
Severe and sweeping, going much further than usual.
Mocking in tone, often by praising what one actually scorns.
Concerned with school life, teaching and study.

mnemonics: Bombastic comes from bombast, cotton stuffing once used to pad out clothes: bombastic speech is padded out with grand words.

senses.definition: Rough and rude in manner, with no sense of what others find polite.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Rude and loud, with bad manners.

examples.text: His boorish table manners embarrassed his hosts throughout the formal dinner.
He talked loudly on his phone in the quiet gallery, and the other visitors glared at the boorish tourist.
He grabbed food off other guests' plates and talked over the speeches, and his boorish behavior was all anyone discussed after the wedding.
The comedian's routine relied too heavily on boorish jokes and crude insults.

distractors.lemma: Happiest with books and study, often more than with people.
Gloomy about the market and expecting share prices to drop.
Youthful in a way that brings to mind a young boy.
So dull that it leaves people weary and restless.
Having a big, solid, muscular body.

mnemonics: A boorish person acts like a wild boar, charging around with crude and bad manners.

senses.definition: Grow, spread or increase quickly and with fresh energy.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To grow fast and spread out, like new leaves in spring.

examples.text: As word of the cheap rents spread, the artists' colony began to burgeon, with new studios opening every month.
Interest in home baking burgeoned during the long winter lockdowns, and flour sold out in many shops.
The city's population burgeoned from twenty thousand to half a million in just three decades.
What began as a stall at a weekend market has burgeoned into a chain of forty shops.

distractors.lemma: Beat down someone's resistance with threats, as if hitting them with a club.
Make metal gleam by rubbing it hard with a cloth or tool.
Break into a house or other building to steal from it.
Load someone down with something heavy or troublesome.
Tunnel into the earth, as rabbits and moles do.

senses.definition: Of a plant, start to sprout new buds and shoots.

mnemonics: Burgeon comes from an old French word for a bud: picture buds bursting open all over a tree in spring, and you have something that burgeons.

senses.definition: Strengthen an argument, position or plan by adding evidence or support that makes it harder to attack.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To back up an idea or plan so it is harder to knock down.

examples.text: The lawyer buttressed her case with phone records showing the defendant was miles away.
New fossil finds buttress the theory that birds descended from small dinosaurs.
The coach hoped two experienced signings would buttress a defense that had leaked goals all season.
To buttress his request for a raise, he brought a list of the projects he had led that year.

distractors.lemma: Stop someone and keep them talking, often to ask a favor.
Make up for an injustice by putting things back the way they should be.
Make someone deeply upset and troubled.
Keep bothering or pressuring someone in an unpleasant way.
Make someone feel foolish or uncomfortable in front of others.

senses.definition: Prop up a wall or building with a solid structure built against its outside.

mnemonics: Buttress comes from an old French word meaning to push against: a stone buttress pushes back against a wall, and evidence can buttress an argument the same way.

senses.definition: A din of loud, clashing sounds with no harmony between them.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A jumble of loud noises that hurts the ears.

examples.text: The orchestra tuning their instruments created a cacophony before the maestro stepped onto the podium.
A sudden cacophony of car horns erupted in the street during the rush hour traffic jam.
Construction work outside the window produced an endless cacophony of metallic clanging.
Three toddlers banging on pots while the dog barked turned the small kitchen into a cacophony.

distractors.lemma: A long work written for a whole orchestra to play, often in four parts.
A sudden moment when something becomes clear to someone.
One of two or more words, like pair and pear, that sound alike but differ in meaning.
Handwriting done as an art, with carefully shaped, elegant letters.
The technology of carrying voices over a distance, as telephones do.

senses.definition: In poetry or prose, a harsh, jarring run of word sounds, often used on purpose.

mnemonics: Cacophony comes from Greek roots kakos (bad) and phone (sound), making it a harsh noise.

senses.definition: Talk someone into doing what they would rather not, using charm, praise and patient pleading.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To get someone to do something by sweet talk and praise.

examples.text: With compliments and promises to do his chores, he tried to cajole his younger sister into sharing her dessert.
The diplomat used charm and patience to cajole the reluctant leaders into signing the treaty.
By praising her past work and asking very sweetly, she managed to cajole the manager into extending her deadline.
Advertisers often cajole consumers into buying luxury items by appealing to their vanity.

distractors.lemma: Ease the sadness of someone who has suffered a loss or a letdown.
Raise small, fussy objections that miss the main point.
Beat someone with a short, thick club.
Work together in secret to cheat or break the law.
Laugh or chatter in a loud, harsh voice, like a hen.

mnemonics: Cajole rhymes with goal: you cajole someone with sweet talk until you reach your goal.

senses.definition: Grown so hard and unfeeling that other people's pain or misfortune stirs no pity.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Not caring at all when other people are hurt or in trouble.

examples.text: The landlord evicted the sick tenant in midwinter with a callous shrug, saying rent was rent.
After years in the emergency room, he worried he had grown callous, since crying patients no longer moved him.
Critics condemned the chief executive's callous jokes about the workers he had just laid off.
Her callous reply to her grieving friend, that everyone dies eventually, ended their friendship.
It is hard to understand how anyone could stay so callous after seeing children go hungry.

distractors.lemma: Young and untested, without the judgment that comes from experience.
Pale and faintly yellow in the face, in a way that suggests poor health.
Bringing sudden ruin, great loss or widespread misery.
Resentful that someone else has advantages or things one wants for oneself.
Tireless and eager in support of a cause, belief or goal.

senses.definition: Having calluses; having skin made tough and thick through wear.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Having skin that has become thick and hard from frequent friction.

examples.text: The old sailor had callous hands from decades of pulling heavy ropes.
Playing the guitar daily left her fingertips thick and callous.
Manual laborers often develop callous palms that protect them from blisters.
The blacksmith rubbed lotion on his callous skin after a long day at the forge.
Calloused skin
With a workman's callous hands

distractors.lemma: Smooth and delicate like silk fabric.
Swollen and inflamed due to an allergic reaction.
Covered in fine microscopic scales.
Pale and translucent from lack of sunlight.
Tender and prone to bruising easily.

mnemonics: Just as a skin callus becomes tough from friction, a callous person has an emotionally hardened heart.

senses.definition: Openness in saying what one really thinks, even when the truth is awkward or unwelcome.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Saying openly and honestly what you really think.

examples.text: She spoke about her past mistakes with surprising candor, hiding nothing from the interviewer.
His candor set him apart from politicians who hid behind scripted, evasive answers.
With unusual candor, the coach admitted that his own poor decisions had cost the team the game.
I valued my editor's candor; she told me plainly that the first three chapters were dull.

distractors.lemma: Resentment that has hardened into lasting hostility toward someone over an old wrong.
Burning eagerness or devotion, as for a person or a cause.
A dreamy, pleasantly lazy feeling, as on a hot afternoon.
A loud ringing noise of metal striking metal, repeated again and again.
A run for elected office, or the state of being a candidate for a post.

senses.definition: Ability to make judgments free from discrimination or dishonesty.

mnemonics: Candor shares a root with candid and candle, Latin candere, to shine: candor lets the plain truth shine through.

senses.definition: Inclined to switch moods or plans suddenly, with nothing to explain the change.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Likely to change suddenly, so you cannot predict what will happen next.

examples.text: The weather in the mountains is capricious, so hikers pack for both sun and snow.
Employees never knew which rule their capricious manager would enforce on a given day.
Investors fled the market, unsettled by capricious swings in interest rates.

distractors.lemma: Large enough inside to hold a great deal.
Greedy, and ready to take by force what belongs to others.
Quick to complain about small and unimportant faults.
Showing promising signs that things will go well.

senses.definition: Determined by chance or impulse or whim rather than by necessity or reason.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Capricious describes actions or decisions driven by sudden whims rather than careful thought.

examples.text: His capricious decision to quit his job shocked all his colleagues.
We fell victim to the capricious whims of the tour guide.
Making large purchases on a whim is a capricious habit.
The king made several capricious decrees that confused the kingdom.
A capricious refusal
Authoritarian rulers are frequently capricious

distractors.lemma: Calculated with extreme mathematical precision.
Derived from logical reasoning and solid evidence.
Planned meticulously over a long period.
Associated with severe legal penalties.
Rooted in ancient traditions and customs.

mnemonics: A capricious person acts on a sudden caprice, shifting their mood or mind without any warning.

senses.definition: Criticize or reprimand someone severely.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To scold or criticize someone very harshly.

examples.text: The coach did not hesitate to castigate the team after their dismal performance.
In her review, she castigated the museum for hiding its best paintings in a basement.
Parents should guide children rather than constantly castigate them.

distractors.lemma: Set something in motion, especially trouble or a conflict.
Chew food before swallowing it.
Examine the facts of something to find out the truth.
Lessen how harsh, painful or serious something is.

senses.definition: Inflict severe punishment on.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To castigate means to punish someone severely for wrongdoing.

examples.text: Ancient legal codes would castigate minor offenses with harsh physical penalties.
The tribunal threatened to castigate any official who accepted bribes.
Monastic rules allowed the abbot to castigate wayward monks.
Society tends to castigate those who violate core moral standards.

distractors.lemma: To heal a wound using herbal medicine.
To cast a bronze statue in a foundry.
To hide a secret treasure in a cave.
To honor a hero with a medal.
To estimate the value of a property.

mnemonics: Castigate comes from the Latin castigare, "to correct or punish": to castigate is to correct someone with harsh words.

senses.definition: Something or someone that causes an important change or event to happen.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A person or thing that starts or speeds up a big change.

examples.text: The factory's closure became the catalyst for a new wave of small businesses in town.
Her blunt question acted as a catalyst, and the meeting finally reached a decision.
Historians see the printing press as a catalyst for the spread of new ideas.

distractors.lemma: A person who studies data or situations in close detail.
A sudden, violent disaster such as a flood or an earthquake.
A complete list of items arranged in a set order.
A machine that hurls heavy objects through the air.
A teacher of religious doctrine who uses questions and answers.

senses.definition: A substance that starts or speeds up a chemical reaction without being changed itself.

mnemonics: Catalyst comes from the Greek katalysis, "dissolving": a catalyst breaks a fixed situation apart so that change can happen.

senses.definition: Harsh or corrosive in tone.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Bitterly sarcastic in a way that is meant to hurt.

examples.text: The critic was known for caustic reviews that could close a play within a week.
She regretted her caustic remarks as soon as she saw his hurt expression.
His caustic wit made him both feared and admired in the boardroom.

distractors.lemma: Having to do with sound, or with the ability to hear it.
Simple and plain in a way typical of the countryside.
Relaxed and informal rather than careful or planned.
Being the reason that something happens.
Unwilling to take risks; acting with great care.

senses.definition: Of a substance, especially a strong acid; capable of destroying or eating away by chemical action.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Able to burn or destroy skin and materials through chemical action.

examples.text: The laboratory technician handled the caustic liquid with extreme caution.
A caustic chemical spill required the immediate evacuation of the science wing.
Protective gloves are mandatory when dealing with caustic substances.
The metal railing began to corrode after being exposed to a caustic solution.

distractors.lemma: Relating to the artistic depiction of coastal landscapes.
Marked by a sarcastic and biting sense of humor.
Tending to cause sudden and unpredictable changes.
Existing as a natural, unrefined mineral compound.
Characterized by rapid physical growth and development.

mnemonics: Caustic comes from the Greek kaustikos, "burning": caustic words burn like acid.

senses.definition: Crafty deception, such as twisting rules, exploiting loopholes or using misleading arguments, to get one's way, especially in law, politics or business.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Sly tricks and misleading talk used to cheat people or get an unfair edge.

examples.text: The broker's financial chicanery, including fake invoices and shell companies, cost elderly investors their savings.
Through procedural chicanery, the senator delayed the vote until half his opponents had gone home.
The landlord used legal chicanery, burying an unfair fee in the fine print, to keep tenants' deposits.
Parents cried chicanery when the school board quietly moved the meeting to a time when most of them were at work.

distractors.lemma: A court that settles disputes by general fairness rather than by the strict letter of the law.
Courteous, protective conduct, especially by men toward women, modeled on the ideals of knights.
Smart, fashionable elegance in how one dresses or carries oneself.
Fancy, eye-catching clothes and jewelry saved for grand occasions.
Machines and their working parts, taken together as a group.

mnemonics: Chicanery comes from the French chicaner, to quibble: it means winning by sly tricks and hair-splitting arguments rather than fair means.

senses.definition: Thicken from a liquid into a soft or solid mass, as blood does when it clots and milk when it curdles.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To change from a runny liquid into a thick or solid mass.

examples.text: Blood begins to coagulate within minutes of a cut, forming a clot that stops the bleeding.
Proteins in egg white coagulate in a hot pan, turning the clear liquid firm and white.
Cheesemakers add rennet to warm milk, which makes it coagulate into soft curds.
Patients on blood thinners bleed longer because their blood takes more time to coagulate.

distractors.lemma: Come together in one place as a group, as people do for worship or a meeting.
Think hard and at length about a problem or idea.
Give the different forms a verb takes for person, number and tense.
Bend a flat sheet into rows of wavy folds, as in cardboard or roofing metal.
Stop holding out and surrender on terms agreed with the other side.

mnemonics: Coagulate comes from Latin coagulum, rennet, the stuff cheesemakers use to curdle milk: to coagulate is to clot or curdle.

senses.definition: Of separate parts, join up and become a single combined mass, group or idea.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To come together and become one group or thing.

examples.text: Raindrops on the window coalesce into larger drops that finally run down the glass.
Over two centuries, the scattered villages coalesced into a single sprawling city.
Several small activist groups coalesced into one national movement after the court ruling.
Her vague worries slowly coalesced into a clear plan to leave the company.
The opposition parties failed to coalesce around one candidate, so the vote split three ways.

distractors.lemma: Go along with a plan or demand without objecting, even while privately unhappy about it.
Rest and slowly regain strength while getting better after an illness or injury.
Fade away bit by bit until nothing is left to see.
Give off a stream of small gas bubbles, as a fizzy drink does.
Push someone into acting against their will by threats or pressure.

mnemonics: Coalesce comes from Latin co-, together, and alescere, to grow: separate parts grow together into one.

senses.definition: Convincing because the reasoning behind it is sound, clear and to the point.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: So clear and sensible that people find it convincing.

examples.text: The defense attorney's cogent argument, built step by step on the evidence, swayed the jury.
The essay was well written but not cogent, since its conclusion did not follow from its evidence.
She made a cogent case for a four-day week, citing data from three trial programs, and the board agreed.
Unable to give a cogent reason for the delay, the contractor simply apologized.
Reviewers praised the book's cogent analysis, which left few readers doubting its conclusions.

distractors.lemma: Aware of something and keeping it in mind.
Related by having the same origin, as words in sister languages often are.
Strong and sharp in smell or taste, enough to sting the nose or tongue.
So poor that one depends on others for food, shelter and other basic needs.
Dependent on a condition that has not yet been settled.

mnemonics: Cogent comes from Latin cogere, to drive together or compel: a cogent argument compels you to agree.

senses.definition: Matching something else in amount, size or degree, so that the two are in fair proportion.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: In the right amount to match something else, like pay that fits the work done.

examples.text: The punishment should be commensurate with the seriousness of the crime, neither harsher nor lighter.
Her vast responsibilities are not commensurate with her modest pay, so she is asking for a raise.
The explorers expected a reward commensurate with the risks they had taken.
A quick apology was hardly commensurate with the damage his lies had done to her career.
The city's spending on flood walls was not commensurate with the danger, and the river broke through.

distractors.lemma: Showing flawless, polished skill, as a true master of a craft does.
Deserving to be praised for its quality or effort.
Offering plenty of room inside, as a large house or cabin does.
Made or done to honor the memory of a person or event.
Living closely alongside another species and feeding from it without doing it harm.

mnemonics: Commensurate shares a root with 'measure'; things that are commensurate have matching measures.

senses.definition: Showing a cheerful willingness to do favors for others.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Eager to please others and quick to go along with their wishes.

examples.text: The complaisant clerk agreed to every change the customer demanded, even the unreasonable ones.
Eager to avoid conflict, the complaisant board approved the chief executive's plans without a single question.
She was complaisant with her in-laws, cheerfully cooking whatever they requested at every holiday.
The complaisant waiter happily moved us to three different tables until we were satisfied.

distractors.lemma: So pleased with oneself or one's situation that one stops watching for risks or trying to improve.
Sharing the guilt for a wrong by having helped to bring it about.
Calm and collected, with feelings kept steady even in a tense moment.
Driven by an inner urge that is hard to resist, often to repeat an act.
Skilled enough to handle a task properly.

mnemonics: Complaisant comes from French complaire, to please: a complaisant person goes out of the way to please others. Do not confuse it with complacent, meaning smug.

senses.definition: Meant to ease anger or hostility and win back someone's goodwill.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Trying to calm someone's anger and make peace.

examples.text: After the heated meeting, the manager sent a conciliatory email apologizing for raising his voice.
Hoping to end the strike, the company made a conciliatory offer of higher wages and an extra holiday.
Her tone turned conciliatory once she realized her neighbor had not meant to damage the fence.
After years of hostility, the two countries exchanged conciliatory gestures, freeing prisoners and reopening the border.

distractors.lemma: Praising someone warmly for a win or a happy event.
Swinging or moving back and forth at a steady rhythm.
Brief and direct, using no more words than needed.
Made up of claims that cannot all be true at once.
Serving to back up or verify something already suggested.

senses.definition: Making or willing to make concessions.

mnemonics: Conciliatory comes from Latin conciliare, to bring together or win over, the root of reconcile: conciliatory words aim to reconcile.

senses.definition: Allow misconduct to go on without objecting to it or punishing it, as if giving it silent approval.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To let bad behavior slide without punishing it.

examples.text: By laughing along at the cruel joke, the manager seemed to condone it.
The principal said the school would not condone cheating, and the students involved were suspended.
Although she understood why he had lied, she could not condone it.
Critics argued that the league's tiny fines effectively condoned violence on the field.
She condoned her husband's occasional affairs, pretending not to notice them for the children's sake.

distractors.lemma: Offer words of sympathy to someone who is mourning a death.
Tend to lead to or help produce a certain result.
Turn from a gas into a liquid, as steam does on a cold window.
Treat others as though one were better or more important than they are.
Puzzle someone so thoroughly that they cannot think straight.

mnemonics: Condone shares a root with donate, Latin donare, to give: when you condone a wrong, you give it a free pass.

senses.definition: A very intense and uncontrolled fire.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A massive and destructive fire that gets out of hand.

examples.text: The dry summer weather sparked a terrifying conflagration in the hills.
The Great Fire of 1666 was a conflagration that burned much of medieval London to the ground.
Firefighters battled all night to contain the raging conflagration.
A single discarded cigarette started a conflagration that gutted the entire warehouse.

distractors.lemma: The act of whipping someone or oneself, often as a religious penance.
The way the parts of something are set out in relation to one another.
A sudden alarm and bewilderment that leaves one unsure what to do.
The people who gather regularly for worship at a particular church.
The act of declaring something holy and setting it apart for worship.

senses.definition: A violent, widespread conflict, such as a war that draws in many nations.

mnemonics: Conflagration comes from Latin conflagrare, to burn up, from flagrare, to blaze: a conflagration is a blaze out of control.

senses.definition: A person with deep knowledge and practiced taste who can judge quality in an art or in luxuries such as food or wine.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Someone who knows a great deal about a fine thing, like wine or art, and can tell good from bad.

examples.text: A tea connoisseur, she could name the region a leaf came from after a single sip.
Only a true connoisseur could spot the tiny brushwork that marked the painting as a forgery.
The wine list was written for connoisseurs, with notes on soil, vintage and grape that most diners skipped.
He is no connoisseur of jazz; to him, every saxophone solo sounds the same.

distractors.lemma: A building caretaker or hotel staff member who watches the door, sorts the mail and helps guests.
A close friend trusted with one's secrets and private worries.
Someone who tells stories with wit and flair, especially at social gatherings.
Someone who builds a new company from scratch and stakes money on its success.
One of a group secretly plotting to do something harmful or illegal.

mnemonics: Connoisseur comes from an old French word meaning to know, related to recognize: a connoisseur knows quality when they see or taste it.

senses.definition: Showing sincere, humble regret for a wrong one has done, along with a wish to make amends.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Deeply sorry for doing something wrong.

examples.text: Head bowed, the defendant looked contrite as he apologized to the victim's family.
The contrite teenager returned the stolen bike and offered to pay for the scratches.
He wrote a contrite letter to the friend he had lied to, asking for forgiveness.
The company's statement sounded more defensive than contrite, and angry customers were not satisfied.

distractors.lemma: Repeated so many times that it now sounds stale and empty, like a tired saying.
Plainly planned or forced, so that it seems artificial instead of natural.
Known or understood only by a few specialists, as obscure learning is.
Pointing or pulling the opposite way from something else.
Real and solid enough to be seen or touched, not abstract.

mnemonics: Contrite comes from Latin contritus, ground down or crushed: a contrite person feels crushed by guilt over a wrong.

senses.definition: A baffling puzzle or situation that seems to have no clear solution.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A tricky problem that is very hard to figure out.

examples.text: Keeping the old bridge open while building a new one beside it was a conundrum that stumped three engineering firms.
Parents face a familiar conundrum: the harder they push a child to read, the less the child wants to.
Why the bees abandoned a healthy hive remained a conundrum that nobody in the beekeeping club could explain.
Fitting six people, two dogs and a piano into a two-bedroom flat posed a conundrum the family argued about for weeks.

distractors.lemma: A tough natural crystal used to grind and polish metal; rubies and sapphires are colored forms of it.
A group of companies or organizations that pool their money and skills for a shared venture.
A smooth range that shades gradually from one extreme to the other with no sharp breaks.
A sudden fit of furious crying, shouting or kicking, as by a small child who is refused something.
The thin layer of skin deep inside the ear that shakes when sound reaches it.

mnemonics: Conundrum ends in drum: a hard puzzle keeps drumming in your head until you work it out.

senses.definition: Winding through so many twists, layers or side steps that it is hard to keep track of.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Twisted and complicated, so it is hard to follow.

examples.text: The tax form's convoluted instructions sent us back to page one three times before we found the right box.
His excuse was so convoluted that by the end nobody could remember why he had missed the flight.
The film's convoluted plot jumps between four timelines, and half the audience was lost by the second hour.
Getting a refund required a convoluted chain of phone calls, emails and signed forms.

distractors.lemma: Warm and cheerful, and fond of shared meals and good company.
Slowly regaining strength after being ill or hurt.
Able to keep up a fast, steady stream of talk with no effort.
Happening on its own, without a person choosing to do it.
Marked by sudden, violent jerks of the muscles.

senses.definition: Coiled or folded back on itself, like a rolled leaf or the ridges of the brain.

mnemonics: Convoluted comes from the Latin convolvere, 'to roll together': a convoluted story is rolled up in so many loops that it is hard to unwind.

senses.definition: Supplied or present in great quantity.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Very large in amount, with lots of it to go around.

examples.text: She took copious notes during the lecture, filling twelve pages before the first break.
The recipe calls for copious amounts of garlic, so buy at least two whole bulbs.
Copious spring rain turned the dry creek bed into a rushing stream within a week.
The vines gave a copious harvest that summer, more tomatoes than the family could ever eat.

distractors.lemma: Fine and in good order, with nothing to worry about.
Easy to notice because it stands out from its surroundings.
Looking convincing at first while hiding a flaw that makes it false.
Prone to sudden, unexplained changes of mind or mood.
Devoted to a religion and careful to follow its practices.

mnemonics: Think of a 'cornucopia', the horn of plenty, to remember that copious means abundant.

senses.definition: Establish or strengthen as with new evidence or facts.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To back up a theory or claim with fresh facts.

examples.text: Two neighbors who heard the crash were able to corroborate the driver's account of the accident.
The reporter refused to publish the claim until a second source could corroborate it.
Phone records corroborated her story that she had been at home all evening.
Letters found in the attic corroborate the family legend that their great-grandfather survived a shipwreck.

distractors.lemma: Eat away at metal or stone slowly, as rust or acid does.
Bend a flat sheet into a row of folds, as in cardboard or roofing metal.
Team up with others on a shared piece of work.
Add more detail to an idea, plan or explanation.
Lead someone into dishonest or immoral behavior, often with bribes.

mnemonics: Corroborate and robust share the Latin robur, 'strength': to corroborate a story is to make it stronger with evidence.

senses.definition: Disposed to believe on little evidence.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Quick to believe things without needing much proof.

examples.text: The credulous boy believed every tale his older cousins told him about a monster living in the lake.
Scam artists often target credulous investors looking for quick riches.
Only a credulous tourist would pay fifty dollars for a "genuine" Roman coin sold from a street cart.
Credulous readers shared the story about free airline tickets without ever asking where it came from.
The ad's miracle diet was so plainly fake that it could fool none but the most credulous shoppers.

distractors.lemma: Believable because it seems honest or likely to be true.
Worthy of some respect or approval, as a solid effort is.
Working steadily and carefully without letting up.
Shaky and unsteady, the way a voice or hand gets when someone is scared or frail.
Always grumbling and finding fault, in a fretful tone.

mnemonics: Credulous comes from the Latin credere, 'to believe', like credit and creed: a credulous person believes too easily.

senses.definition: Hasty and without attention to detail; not thorough.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Done very quickly and without paying attention to important details.

examples.text: Even a cursory glance at the contract was enough to spot the extra fees.
She gave the manuscript only a cursory read before rejecting it, skipping most of the middle chapters.
The detective's search of the room was cursory, and he missed the letter taped under the drawer.
He offered a cursory apology without looking up from his phone and hurried out the door.
After a cursory five-minute inspection, the buyer signed off on a house with a cracked foundation.

distractors.lemma: Drifting across many side topics rather than following one line of thought.
Handwritten so that the letters run into one another without the pen lifting.
Under a curse, or so hateful that it seems to deserve one.
Coming before an event and hinting that it is on the way.
Seeming real while having no basis in fact.

mnemonics: Cursory comes from the Latin cursor, 'runner', like the cursor that races across a screen: a cursory look runs past the details.

senses.definition: A serious shortage, where there is far too little of something that is needed or wanted.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Not nearly enough of something; a real shortage.

examples.text: After months without rain there was a dearth of fresh water, and villagers walked miles to fill a single bucket.
The town has such a dearth of doctors that patients often wait three months for an appointment.
Despite all the hype, the comedy suffered from a dearth of good jokes, and I laughed maybe twice.
A dearth of reliable records from that century makes it hard to say how many people lived in the valley.

distractors.lemma: The point at which a living thing stops living for good.
The paved area in front of and under a fireplace.
How wide something is, measured across from one edge to the other.
The size of something measured all the way around it, as with a tree trunk or a waist.
Laughter and lighthearted fun.

mnemonics: Dearth is built from dear plus -th, like warmth from warm: when food is scarce, it grows dear, meaning costly.

senses.definition: An event or plan that collapses into total failure, often in a way that embarrasses everyone involved.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Something that goes so badly wrong it becomes an embarrassing mess.

examples.text: The product launch was a debacle: the website crashed, the demo failed and the CEO apologized on stage.
After the debacle of last year's picnic, when a storm blew every tent into the lake, the club booked an indoor hall.
The army's retreat became a debacle as soldiers abandoned their guns and fled in panic.
Critics called the botched vote count a debacle that left people trusting the system even less.

distractors.lemma: The first time a performer, athlete or product is shown to the public.
A contest of arguments in which two sides take turns making their case for and against an idea.
An entry in an account that records money taken out or owed.
A small sea creature with a hard shell that glues itself to rocks and ship hulls.
A bout of wild partying and heavy drinking.

senses.definition: Flooding caused by a tumultuous breakup of ice in a river during the spring or summer.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Flooding caused by broken ice rushing down a river.

examples.text: Spring brought the annual debacle that threatened the wooden bridge.
Villagers prepared their homes for the destructive river debacle.
The ice jam melted rapidly, creating a dangerous debacle.
Engineers monitored the spring debacle to prevent flooding.

distractors.lemma: A dry period of extreme heat and little rain.
A gentle shower of autumn leaves.
A thick layer of morning fog over the hills.
A calm ocean tide at midnight.
A steady stream of underground water.

mnemonics: Debacle comes from a French word for river ice breaking up: picture a frozen plan cracking apart all at once.

senses.definition: Prove that a popular story, claim or reputation is untrue or overblown, usually by laying out the facts against it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To prove that something many people believe is wrong.

examples.text: The museum's new exhibit debunks the old myth that Vikings wore horned helmets into battle.
A simple test with two glasses of tap water was enough to debunk the salesman's miracle filter.
Fact-checkers rushed to debunk the viral photo, showing it had been taken years earlier in another country.
The physicist debunked the psychic's claims by repeating each trick with an ordinary deck of cards.

distractors.lemma: Step ashore or off an aircraft once the journey is over.
Sleep somewhere makeshift, often for just a night or two.
Cheapen something by lowering its quality or moral worth.
Drain someone's strength and leave them feeble.
Question someone in detail after a mission or task.

mnemonics: To debunk a rumor is to remove the 'bunk' or nonsense from it.

senses.definition: Conduct that keeps to good manners and suits the seriousness of the occasion.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Polite, respectful behavior that fits a formal place or event.

examples.text: The judge warned that anyone who shouted again would be removed, since the courtroom demanded decorum.
Even when the groom's friends began heckling, the bride's grandmother kept her decorum and smiled politely.
Breaches of decorum at the royal court, such as turning your back on the queen, could end a career.
The rowdy fans showed little decorum, throwing popcorn and booing during the moment of silence.

distractors.lemma: The look a room gets from its colors, furniture and ornaments.
A fake animal or other lure used to draw prey or people into a trap.
A formal command from a ruler or court that has the force of law.
The minimum attendance a group's rules require before its votes count.
A meeting, website or other setting where people trade views on a subject.

mnemonics: Decorum comes from the Latin decorus, 'fitting' or 'proper': decorum is behavior that fits the occasion.

senses.definition: The habit or act of giving way to someone else, out of respect for their age, rank or knowledge.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Letting someone else decide or have their way because you respect them.

examples.text: In deference to her grandmother's wishes, she wore a dress to the wedding instead of jeans.
Out of deference to the senior surgeon, the junior doctors waited for her to speak before offering any opinion.
His deference to his older brother was so complete that he never made a decision without asking him first.
The committee showed little deference to the mayor and rejected her plan outright.

distractors.lemma: A point or quality that makes one thing unlike another.
A delay of something, such as a payment or military service, to a later date.
A conclusion worked out from clues or evidence rather than stated directly.
A planned gathering, often lasting several days, where people meet to share ideas on a field.
The act of meddling in something in a way that hinders it.

senses.definition: Courteous regard for people's feelings.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Being thoughtful and polite about other people's feelings.

examples.text: He lowered his voice out of deference to the sleeping infant.
She chose her words with careful deference to his sensitive nature.
His gentle reply was shaped by deference to her recent loss.
They adjusted the schedule in deference to the weary travelers.
In deference to your wishes

distractors.lemma: A strong preference for spicy food.
The act of differing from the majority opinion.
A lack of clarity in legal documents.
The careful preservation of historical artifacts.

mnemonics: Deference comes from defer, 'to yield': showing deference means you defer to someone else's wishes.

senses.definition: Damaging to health, to living things or to the proper working of something.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Doing damage or harm, especially to health.

examples.text: Years of road salt had a deleterious effect on the bridge's steel supports, which were badly rusted.
Doctors warn that heavy drinking can be deleterious to a teenager's developing brain.
The new pesticide proved deleterious to bees, and hive numbers fell by half within a season.
Skipping sleep before an exam has a deleterious effect on memory, so cramming all night often backfires.

distractors.lemma: Confused and restless, often seeing or saying strange things, as during a high fever.
So tasty that it is a real pleasure to eat or drink.
Meant and planned ahead, not happening by accident.
Fine and dainty in texture, structure or flavor.
Wanting or hoping for something very much.

mnemonics: Deleterious begins with delete: something deleterious can wipe out your health bit by bit.

senses.definition: Speak of someone or something with mocking scorn, as if it deserved no respect.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To mock or make fun of someone in a mean way.

examples.text: Classmates derided his homemade costume, pointing and laughing until he left the party.
Early critics derided the Impressionists as careless amateurs who could not finish a painting.
Online commenters derided the new logo, calling it a child's scribble and posting cruel parodies of it.
It is easy to deride a beginner's clumsy first attempts, but mocking them only makes people quit.

distractors.lemma: Get something, such as pleasure or an idea, from a particular source.
Keep someone from having something they need or want.
Throw a person's mind or an orderly system into confusion.
Lead someone to believe something that is false.
Ruin the look of a wall, sign or statue by scratching, marking or painting over it.

mnemonics: Deride comes from Latin ridere, to laugh, the root of ridicule: to deride people is to laugh them down.

senses.definition: Copied or adapted from the work of others; not original.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Copying other people's ideas instead of offering something new.

examples.text: Critics dismissed the novel as derivative, little more than a rewrite of older thrillers.
The band's early songs were derivative, but their second album found its own sound.
Investors wanted something new, not another derivative app that copied a popular game.

distractors.lemma: Added to make something look nicer rather than to be useful.
Final and settled, leaving no room for doubt.
Expressing contempt or ridicule.
Very small in size.
Relating to careful discussion before a decision.

mnemonics: Derivative work is derived from someone else's: it repeats rather than creates.

senses.definition: Dry something out completely, drawing off every bit of its moisture.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To make something totally dry, for example to keep food from going bad.
