senses.definition: Having or revealing little emotion or sensibility; not easily aroused or excited.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Showing no emotion or reaction even in difficult situations.

examples.text: Her impassive expression made it impossible to guess whether she liked the offer.
The judge remained impassive as the verdict was read, even while the courtroom erupted in shouts and tears.
Even when the crowd booed, the umpire's face stayed impassive, giving no hint of anger or hurt.
Poker players learn to look impassive so that opponents cannot read their hands from their faces.
He heard the bad news in impassive silence, which worried friends who had expected him to weep.

distractors.lemma: Blocked or rough enough that no one can cross or travel through it.
Inclined to act on sudden urges without thinking first.
Playfully naughty, like a mischievous child.
Of enormous size, weight or bulk.
Rude and cheeky in a bold, disrespectful way.

mnemonics: Impassive joins im-, not, to the Latin root of passion (pati, to suffer or feel): an impassive face shows no passion.

senses.definition: Not having enough money to pay for necessities.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Short of money, often barely able to get by.

examples.text: As an impecunious student, he lived on rice and beans and walked everywhere to save bus fare.
The impecunious count sold the family paintings one by one to pay for repairs to the roof.
An impecunious traveler arrived at the inn with barely enough coins for a single loaf of bread.
Impecunious young artists in the city often crowd into small apartments to split the rent.

distractors.lemma: Acting suddenly, without stopping to think.
Without a single flaw or mistake.
Having to do with money.
Lacking reverence for what is holy.

mnemonics: Impecunious holds Latin pecunia, "money", as in pecuniary; the im- means without, so it means without money.

senses.definition: Commanding others with an arrogant air, as though their obedience were owed.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Bossy and proud, acting as if everyone must do what you say.

examples.text: With an imperious wave of her hand, the duchess sent the servants scurrying from the room.
He snapped his fingers at the waiter in an imperious way that made everyone at the table cringe.
The new director's imperious memos, full of orders and deadlines, never once asked for anyone's opinion.
Used to command, the retired general spoke to his grandchildren in the same imperious tone he had used on his troops.

distractors.lemma: Likely to lead to injury or disaster.
So slight that it can hardly be seen or felt.
Able to last for ages without rotting or fading.
Fake or false, though made to look genuine.

mnemonics: Imperious comes from Latin imperium, "command", the root of empire: an imperious person gives orders like an emperor.

senses.definition: Rude in a cheeky way, especially toward someone owed respect, such as an elder or a superior.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Cheeky and rude to someone you should treat with respect.

examples.text: The impertinent intern corrected the chief executive's grammar in front of the whole board.
My grandmother would not tolerate impertinent answers, and any child who talked back was sent from the table.
He thought it impertinent of a stranger to ask how much money he earned.
The butler raised an eyebrow at the impertinent guest who demanded a tour of the owner's private study.

distractors.lemma: Bound to end or fade after a while.
Feeling no regret for wrongs one has done.
Lacking the power to change a situation.
Coming and going rather than continuing without a break.
Stubbornly determined to keep going until a goal is reached.

senses.definition: Not pertinent to the matter under consideration.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Having nothing to do with the topic you are currently discussing.

examples.text: The attorney objected because the opposing counsel raised impertinent details.
He introduced several impertinent facts that confused the main argument.
The committee dismissed the suggestion as entirely impertinent to the agenda.
Please remove these impertinent remarks from the final report.
Mentioned several impertinent facts before finally coming to the point

distractors.lemma: Extremely important to the final outcome.
Relating directly to personal property rights.
Incapable of being measured accurately.
Showing persistent effort despite obstacles.
Derived from incorrect mathematical assumptions.

mnemonics: Impertinent is in- (not) plus pertinent, relevant: an impertinent remark was first one that did not belong, and the word came to mean cheeky.

senses.definition: Not affected or influenced by something, such as criticism, argument or pain.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Not bothered or changed by something, such as criticism or pain.

examples.text: He remained completely impervious to their harsh criticism and insults.
The dictator seemed impervious to world opinion, shrugging off every sanction and protest.
Years of night shifts had made her impervious to noise; she could sleep through a fire alarm.
Teenagers can seem impervious to advice, then quietly follow it months later.

distractors.lemma: Expecting others to obey at once, in a haughty way.
Quick to act on impulse, without weighing the risks.
Present throughout, reaching into every corner.
Having to do with an empire or an emperor.
So faint or slow that no one picks up on it.

senses.definition: Not allowing water, air or other matter to pass through.

mnemonics: Impervious comes from Latin per, "through", and via, "way"; with im- in front, nothing finds a way through.

senses.definition: Impossible to calm or win over, especially in anger or hostility.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Impossible to calm down, satisfy, or make friendly.

examples.text: The rival faction proved implacable despite numerous attempts at mediation.
She held an implacable grudge against her former business partner.
No amount of reasoning could soften his implacable stance on the issue.
Apologies, flowers and a handwritten letter all failed; her sister remained implacable.

distractors.lemma: Fitting or relevant to a given case.
Hard to believe because it seems unlikely.
Too faint or fine to be felt by touch.
Understood from hints or context rather than said in words.
Pleasant enough to eat or accept.

mnemonics: Implacable shares Latin placare, "to calm", with placate and placid; im- means not, so it cannot be calmed.

senses.definition: Hold a person or thing responsible for an act or quality, usually a bad one such as a fault or a selfish motive.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To claim that someone caused something or has some quality, often a bad one.

examples.text: The crash report did not impute any blame to the pilot, pointing instead to a faulty sensor.
Critics were quick to impute the company's losses to its new chief executive, though the slump began years earlier.
We should not impute selfish motives to her gift just because she mentioned it in a speech.
Readers often impute a narrator's opinions to the author, which annoys many novelists.

distractors.lemma: Openly question whether a claim or a person's character can be trusted.
Soak or fill something thoroughly with a feeling, quality or color.
Pass on knowledge or news to another person.
Slow down or block progress by getting in the way.
Cut off an arm, leg, finger or toe in an operation.

senses.definition: In law or accounting, assign a value to something by estimating it from other figures.

mnemonics: Impute shares a root with compute: Latin putare, 'to reckon'. To impute is to reckon a fault into someone's account.

senses.definition: Not yet fully shaped or organized; still rough and unclear in form.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Still rough and unformed, like an idea you cannot yet put into words.

examples.text: The architect showed an inchoate sketch of the museum, a few loose shapes she would refine into blueprints over the next year.
The author struggled to turn her inchoate thoughts into a clear, ordered chapter.
The protesters shared an inchoate anger that had not yet hardened into specific demands.
Her plan for the business was still inchoate: she had a name and a logo but no idea what to sell.

distractors.lemma: Present in a person or animal from birth rather than learned.
Not alive, like a stone or a chair.
In human form; embodied in a living person.
Going well past what good sense would allow, as with an amount of time or money.
Kept safe from harm, attack or change.

mnemonics: Inchoate comes from Latin incohare, 'to begin': an inchoate plan has only just been started and has no shape yet.

senses.definition: Just starting to show itself, often as the first sign of something that will grow.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Only just beginning to appear or happen.

examples.text: Officers heard the first grumbling in the barracks and moved to crush the incipient rebellion before it spread.
The doctor caught the cancer while it was still incipient, so a small operation was enough.
An incipient smile tugged at her mouth as she read the first line of the letter.
Economists saw rising home sales as a sign of an incipient recovery after two hard years.

distractors.lemma: Weak in flavor and dull to the senses.
Quick to notice and understand things others miss.
Going on without any break or pause.
Owing more money than one can pay back.
Demanding something firmly and refusing to give up.

mnemonics: Incipient comes from Latin incipere, 'to begin' (in- 'on' + capere 'to take'): something incipient is just taking hold.

senses.definition: Poor enough to need help from others.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: So poor that you cannot pay for basic needs without help.

examples.text: The charitable foundation provides food and shelter for indigent families in the city.
Legal aid lawyers represent indigent defendants who cannot afford private counsel.
The clinic treats indigent patients free of charge and pays for it through donations.
Once a wealthy merchant, he died indigent, and the parish paid for his funeral.

distractors.lemma: Angry at something that seems unfair or insulting.
Belonging to a place by origin, not brought there from somewhere else.
Inclined to let others have whatever they want.
Careful and hard-working in carrying out one's duties.
Refusing to change one's position or meet others halfway.

mnemonics: Indigent comes from Latin indigere, 'to be in need': indigent people need help just to get by.

senses.definition: Disinclined to work or exertion.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Lazy and happy to avoid any work or effort.

examples.text: His indolent attitude toward his studies, skipping lectures and never opening a book, led to failing grades.
She spent an indolent summer afternoon dozing in a hammock while the weeds took over the garden.
Once he had tenure, the professor grew indolent and reused the same lecture notes for twenty years.
An indolent employee will rarely volunteer for demanding projects.

distractors.lemma: Rude and openly disrespectful, especially toward people in charge.
Smelling strongly of something.
Sad and gloomy in look or manner.
Unwilling to accept views or behavior different from one's own.
Lacking money for food, rent and other necessities.

senses.definition: Of a disease such as a tumor, growing slowly and causing little or no pain.

mnemonics: Indolent comes from Latin in- 'not' + dolere 'to feel pain': the indolent avoid the pain of hard work. Doctors still call a slow, painless tumor indolent.

senses.definition: Defying expression or description.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: So strong or wonderful that words cannot capture it.

examples.text: She gazed at the sunset over the canyon with ineffable awe.
The symphony left the audience with an ineffable sense of peace that nobody could quite describe afterward.
Asked to describe holding her newborn daughter, she gave up and said the joy was ineffable.
The mystic spoke of an ineffable truth that lay beyond the reach of language.

distractors.lemma: Failing to produce the result that was wanted.
Using more time, money or effort than a task should need.
Not allowed to take part or be chosen because of a rule.
Unsafe or too unpleasant to eat.
Warm and pleasant in manner, and easy to approach.

senses.definition: Too sacred to be uttered.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A word or concept is too sacred and holy to be spoken aloud.

examples.text: Ancient traditions regarded the true name of the deity as ineffable.
The priests guarded the ineffable title with absolute secrecy.
Uttering the ineffable word was strictly forbidden inside the inner sanctum.
The sacred text contained several ineffable passages meant only for silent meditation.
The ineffable name of the Deity

distractors.lemma: Widely spoken by the general public during festivals.
Printed clearly on the exterior walls of the temple.
Translated into multiple modern dialects for education.
Considered offensive by members of the clergy.
Associated with dark magic and curses.

mnemonics: Ineffable comes from Latin in- 'not' + effari 'to speak out': something ineffable cannot be spoken.

senses.definition: Moving forward in a way that nothing can stop or turn aside.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: So steady and strong that nothing can stop it.

examples.text: Year by year, the glacier made its inexorable advance down the valley, burying the old hiking trail.
No new law could halt the inexorable rise in rents once the tech firms moved into the neighborhood.
Despite every effort to save the factory, its decline proved inexorable.
Rising sea levels pose an inexorable threat to towns along the coast.

distractors.lemma: So tangled up with something that the two cannot be pulled apart.
Impossible to explain or make sense of.
Impossible to forgive or defend, whatever explanation is offered.
Far higher than is fair, as with a price or a fee.
So plentiful that it can never be used up.

senses.definition: Not to be placated or appeased or moved by entreaty.

mnemonics: Inexorable comes from Latin in- 'not' + exorare 'to win over by pleading' (orare, 'to pray'): no prayer can stop it.

senses.definition: Openly honest and sincere, without any wish or skill to hide things.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Honest and trusting, like a child who does not know how to hide things.

examples.text: With an ingenuous grin, the boy admitted he had eaten every cookie and asked whether there were more.
An ingenuous child cannot hide his disappointment when he unwraps a boring gift.
Her ingenuous questions about how the scheme worked made it obvious she had played no part in the fraud.
The detective was disarmed by his ingenuous confession, which held nothing back.

distractors.lemma: Showing a gift for inventing new and clever ways to do things.
Thin and easily broken, as with a weak link or a shaky claim.
Taking a lot of hard physical or mental work.
Winding and bending, like a snake or a mountain road.
Firmly fixed and hard to change, as with a habit.

senses.definition: Lacking in sophistication or worldliness.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Being innocent and simple because you have not experienced much of the world yet.

examples.text: His ingenuous belief in human goodness faded after living in the metropolis.
She held an ingenuous view of how politics actually functioned.
The rustic traveler made several ingenuous remarks about city architecture.
Youthful enthusiasm often masks an ingenuous understanding of complex economics.
His ingenuous explanation that he would not have burned the church if he had not thought the bishop was in it

distractors.lemma: Possessing vast knowledge of international art and cuisine.
Showing extreme hostility toward unfamiliar customs.
Marked by bitter cynicism born of frequent betrayal.
Endowed with exceptional mathematical prowess.
Characterized by elaborate and expensive tastes.

mnemonics: Ingenuous comes from Latin ingenuus, 'freeborn' and so 'frank'. Hear genuine inside it: an ingenuous person is genuine, with nothing hidden.

senses.definition: Harmful to something, or tending to hold back its growth or success.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Bad for something, making it hard for it to grow or do well.

examples.text: Layers of paperwork are inimical to small businesses, which cannot afford a compliance team.
The harsh desert climate is inimical to most forms of plant life.
High humidity can prove inimical to delicate electronic instruments.
Constant interruptions are inimical to the deep focus that good writing needs.

distractors.lemma: Unique in a way that no one else can match or imitate.
Kept to the smallest amount needed.
Close and personal, as between old friends.
Full of life, energy and lively movement.
Cool and detached, showing no feeling.

senses.definition: Feeling or showing ill will toward a person or group.

mnemonics: Inimical comes from Latin inimicus, 'enemy' (in- 'not' + amicus 'friend'): something inimical acts like an enemy.

senses.definition: Wicked conduct, especially cruel injustice done to others.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Very wicked or unfair behavior that seriously wrongs people.

examples.text: The preacher thundered against the iniquity of landlords who evicted widows in the dead of winter.
The reporter exposed the iniquity of a prison system that kept children in solitary confinement.
Rigging the water contracts so that the poorest districts paid double was an iniquity the new mayor vowed to undo.
The tyrant's iniquity knew no limits: he jailed critics without trial and seized their farms.

distractors.lemma: The far distant past, such as the time of ancient Greece and Rome.
The state of seeming to be found everywhere at once.
An official investigation into what happened and why.
Money that arrives in equal yearly payments, often until the person receiving it dies.
Skill at inventing clever solutions.

mnemonics: Iniquity comes from Latin iniquus, 'unjust' (in- 'not' + aequus 'equal, fair'): iniquity treats people in a cruelly unfair way.

senses.definition: Causing no harm, and unlikely to upset or offend anyone.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Harmless, and not likely to bother anyone.

examples.text: The question sounded innocuous, but it was a trap meant to make the witness contradict herself.
He made an innocuous comment about the weather to break the tension.
Despite its fearsome fangs, the snake is innocuous; its venom is too weak to hurt a person.
The email looked innocuous, just a simple invoice, until the attachment installed a virus.

distractors.lemma: Hard to spot because it does not stand out.
Out of place or odd next to what surrounds it.
So many that nobody could count them all.
Empty of ideas or real thought.
Showing adult skills or interests at an unusually early age.

mnemonics: Innocuous comes from Latin in- 'not' + nocuus 'harmful', from nocere 'to harm' (as in noxious): innocuous things do no harm.

senses.definition: Weak and dull, with little flavor, energy or interest.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Bland and dull, with no real flavor or spark.

examples.text: The unseasoned broth tasted insipid until the cook added salt, garlic and lemon.
The film's insipid dialogue made even its talented cast sound bored.
After a decade of insipid pop songs, critics welcomed a band with something sharp to say.
A fine wine should never taste insipid or watery on the palate.

distractors.lemma: Only beginning to show, and likely to grow larger.
Spreading slowly and quietly, doing harm before anyone notices.
Brave enough to face danger without fear.
Perfectly clear, as with still water or simple prose.

mnemonics: Insipid comes from Latin in- 'not' + sapidus 'tasty' (from sapere 'to taste', the root of savor): insipid things have no savor.

senses.definition: Narrow in outlook, caring only about one's own small world and wary of anything from beyond it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Cut off from the wider world and not curious about it.

examples.text: The village was so insular that a family who moved there twenty years ago is still called the newcomers.
Critics said the firm's insular culture, where executives hired only old friends, left it blind to new rivals.
Having never traveled or read foreign news, he held insular views about how the rest of the world lived.
Academic fields can become insular when scholars write only for one another.

distractors.lemma: Impossible to dissolve, or impossible to solve.
Meant to hurt or offend someone's feelings.
Refusing to obey the people in charge.
Too annoying or unpleasant to put up with.

senses.definition: Relating to or characteristic of or situated on an island.

mnemonics: Insular comes from Latin insula, 'island' (as in peninsula): insular people live as if on an island, cut off from everyone else.

senses.definition: Resisting every effort to control, cure, or solve it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: So stubborn or tangled that nothing you try seems to fix or control it.

examples.text: After forty years of failed peace talks, the border dispute looked intractable.
His back pain proved intractable: neither surgery nor three different medications brought any relief.
The intractable mule refused to budge, no matter how hard the farmer pulled on the rope.
Homelessness in the city seemed intractable until a new housing program cut it in half within five years.

distractors.lemma: Whole and undamaged, with nothing missing or broken.
Leaving no legal will at the time of one's death.
Able to be pulled back into a housing when not in use.
Responding to what a user does, so that information passes both ways.

mnemonics: Intractable comes from Latin tractare, to handle: an intractable problem is one nobody can get a handle on.

senses.definition: Refusing to give ground or accept any compromise, however strong the arguments or appeals.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Refusing to budge or meet the other side halfway, no matter what.

examples.text: The landlord stayed intransigent, rejecting every offer to split the cost of the repairs.
Talks collapsed after twelve hours because both sides remained intransigent on the pension question.
Her intransigent refusal to consider any other venue meant the wedding had to wait a full year.
No amount of evidence moved the intransigent senator, who voted against the bill for the sixth time.

distractors.lemma: Passing quickly and not staying around for long.
Describing a verb that takes no direct object.
Rising up in armed revolt against a government.
Happening in fits, with gaps between the bursts.
Part of the basic nature of a thing rather than added from outside.

mnemonics: Intransigent comes via Spanish from Latin transigere, to settle a deal. Add in- (not) and you get someone who will not settle.

senses.definition: Load someone with far more of something, such as requests or work, than they can deal with.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To bury someone under a flood of things, like calls, emails, or tasks.

examples.text: After the ad aired, viewers inundated the station with complaints, and the phone lines jammed for hours.
Fans inundated the singer's inbox with so many messages that her account stopped loading.
New managers are often inundated with paperwork in their first weeks, leaving little time to meet the team.
During tax season, accountants are inundated with so many last-minute clients that they barely sleep.
After the newspaper ran its story, the shelter was inundated with donated coats and had to rent a storage unit.

distractors.lemma: Bring in a new method, product or way of doing something.
Suggest something unflattering through hints rather than saying it outright.
Rise and fall in a gentle, rolling pattern, like waves on a lake.
Hold eggs or cultures at a steady warmth so they can develop.

senses.definition: Fill or cover completely, usually with water.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To completely submerge an area in water.

examples.text: Rising tides threaten to inundate the coastal village by midnight.
The broken dam began to inundate the surrounding farmlands.
Torrential downpours can inundate city streets within minutes.
Melting snow will soon inundate the valley floor.

distractors.lemma: To illuminate a dark room with bright artificial lights.
To insulate a house against extreme winter temperatures.
To incinerate waste materials in a large industrial furnace.
To infiltrate a secure facility using forged credentials.

mnemonics: Inundate comes from Latin unda, a wave: to inundate is to send wave after wave over something.

senses.definition: Locked into a habit, often a bad one, by years of repeating it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Doing something so often that it has become a permanent habit.

examples.text: An inveterate gambler, he has bet on the horses every Saturday for forty years and cannot imagine stopping.
My grandfather is an inveterate tinkerer; for six decades he has taken apart every clock he could find.
He is an inveterate liar who has invented stories about himself since childhood, so no one believes his latest tale.
The politician's inveterate habit of interrupting, formed over thirty years of debates, annoyed even his allies.

distractors.lemma: Having no backbone or spinal column.
Turned upside down or placed in reverse order.
Kept free from harm, breach or disrespect.
Able to devise things that nobody had thought of before.
Out of all proportion to what makes sense.

mnemonics: Inveterate shares the Latin root veter-, old, with veteran: an inveterate habit is a veteran habit that has grown old with you.

senses.definition: Quickly aroused to anger.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Easily made angry over very small things.

examples.text: The irascible old neighbor shouted at any child whose ball landed on his lawn.
Even a two-minute delay could set off the irascible manager, who once threw a stapler over a typo.
The chef grew irascible whenever the kitchen fell behind, snapping at anyone who asked a question.
Weeks of poor sleep left her irascible, and she lost her temper at the slightest noise.

distractors.lemma: Able to be rubbed out or wiped clean.
So foolish that it invites laughter.
Driven by feeling or impulse instead of sound logic.
Too tempting or strong to be refused or held back.
Shimmering with colors that shift as you change your angle of view.

mnemonics: Irascible and irate both come from Latin ira, anger: an irascible person turns irate at the smallest thing.

senses.definition: Moving from town to town rather than staying in one place, usually to find or do work.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Always on the move from one place to the next, often for a job.

examples.text: Itinerant farmworkers follow the harvest, picking strawberries in one state in May and apples in another in October.
The itinerant preacher rode from village to village and rarely slept in the same bed twice in a week.
Before radio, itinerant musicians carried news and songs from one market town to the next.
As an itinerant judge, she traveled a circuit of six rural courthouses, holding trials in each for a week.

distractors.lemma: Repeating a process in rounds, each one building on the last.
Built into the nature of something from the start.
Filling a gap for a while until something permanent is ready.
Never making mistakes; wholly free of error.

mnemonics: Itinerant shares the Latin root iter, a journey, with itinerary: an itinerant worker's whole life is an itinerary.

senses.definition: Sparing with words, giving short replies that can seem dry or blunt.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Using very few words to get a point across.

examples.text: His laconic reply, a single 'No,' left no doubt about what he thought of the plan.
The general sent a laconic report of the victory in three words: 'Town is ours.'
The laconic rancher answered the reporter's long questions with a nod, a shrug, or 'Yep.'
Readers love the novel's laconic hero, who says in five words what other characters take a page to say.

distractors.lemma: Showing little effort or enthusiasm; half-hearted and careless.
Inclined to cry easily, or tending to bring on tears.
Having to do with milk or a substance made from it.
Widely seen as a symbol of a time, place or movement.

mnemonics: Laconic comes from Laconia, home of the Spartans, who were famous for short replies. To a king's threat beginning 'If I invade,' they answered only 'If.'

senses.definition: A drained, heavy feeling, physical or mental, that takes away the will to do anything.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A heavy, tired feeling that makes you not want to do anything.

examples.text: Weeks after the fever broke, a lingering lassitude kept him on the sofa, too tired even to read.
The August heat brought a lassitude over the town, and shopkeepers dozed behind their counters.
After the marathon she felt a deep lassitude, as if her legs and her will had both run out.
The long gray winter filled him with a lassitude that made even answering email feel like a chore.

distractors.lemma: The amount of freedom a person is allowed within a set of rules.
Time spent alone, away from other people, often by choice.
Lack of strictness or care in applying rules.
A framework of crossed strips with open spaces between them.
A gap or missing section, as in a manuscript or argument.

senses.definition: A deep stupor close to a coma, as in sleeping sickness.

mnemonics: Lassitude comes from Latin lassus, weary: lassitude is a weariness so deep that it drains the will to act.

senses.definition: Express warm admiration for, especially in speeches, reviews or other public statements.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To praise or honor someone greatly.

examples.text: The committee met to laud the young researcher, whose discovery had changed how the disease is treated.
Critics who once mocked the band now laud its early albums as classics.
Citizens filled the square to laud the rescuers returning from the mountain.
Historians still laud his patient diplomacy, which ended the war without another shot fired.

distractors.lemma: Load goods or cargo onto a ship or vehicle.
Refer to something indirectly, without naming it outright.
Linger in a public place without any clear reason for being there.
Pass illegally earned money through other businesses to hide where it came from.
Stuff a speech or piece of writing with too much of something, such as quotations.

mnemonics: Laud comes from Latin laus, praise, as does laudable. Applaud has a different root, but it still helps: to laud someone is to applaud them with words.

senses.definition: Deficient in alertness or activity.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Sluggish and lacking energy or alertness.

examples.text: Weeks after the flu, he was still lethargic, napping twice a day and struggling to climb the stairs.
The usually playful puppy seemed lethargic, lying in its bed and ignoring the ball.
A heavy lunch often leaves people drowsy and lethargic by mid-afternoon.
Bullfrogs become lethargic as the first cold nights arrive, barely moving at the bottom of the pond.

distractors.lemma: Deadly enough to kill.
Reacting badly in the body to a substance such as pollen or nuts.
Relating to the set forms of public worship.
Expressing deep personal feeling in a graceful, song-like way.

mnemonics: Lethargic comes from Greek lethe, forgetfulness, the name of the river of forgetting in the Greek underworld: a lethargic person seems to have forgotten how to get moving.

senses.definition: Humor or playfulness brought into a situation that is solemn or tense.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Joking around or acting silly when people expect you to be serious.

examples.text: Her giggling during the funeral struck the mourners as a shocking display of levity.
The diplomat injected a moment of levity into the tense negotiations with a joke about the bad coffee.
The judge warned the defendant that his smirks and wisecracks showed a levity the courtroom would not tolerate.
After hours of grim budget cuts, the intern's cartoon of the boss as a superhero brought welcome levity.

distractors.lemma: Gentleness in judging or punishing someone who has done wrong.
Shortness of length or duration, especially in speech or writing.
The span of years that someone lives, or that something keeps working.
A tax or charge that an authority collects.

senses.definition: Physical lightness, the property of having little weight.

mnemonics: Levity comes from Latin levis, light, the same root behind elevate and lever: levity is a light touch where weight is expected.

senses.definition: Fond of talking and quick to fill any silence with conversation.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Liking to talk a lot, often for longer than others want.

examples.text: The loquacious host kept the dinner guests entertained with endless stories about his travels.
Her loquacious nature made it difficult for anyone else to get a word in during meetings.
Seated next to a remarkably loquacious stranger on the train, he barely had time to read.
The loquacious barber chatted happily while trimming his hair.

distractors.lemma: Able to express ideas in a fluent, moving and persuasive way.
So sweet and juicy that it is a delight to eat.
Roomy, with space to hold a great deal.
Heavy with sorrow, often in a showy, overdone way.
Eager to eat or take in large amounts.

mnemonics: Loquacious comes from Latin loqui, to speak, also found in eloquent and soliloquy: a loquacious person speaks and speaks.

senses.definition: Written or spoken in a way that makes even hard ideas simple to grasp.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: So clear that anyone can follow it without effort.

examples.text: After three confusing lectures, the guest speaker's lucid explanation finally made the tax rules make sense to everyone.
Her lucid prose turns dense court rulings into something a high school student could follow.
The instructions were so lucid that I put the bookcase together without once checking the diagrams.
Even under hostile questioning, the witness gave a lucid, step-by-step account of what she had seen that night.

distractors.lemma: Described in shocking, sensational detail, often dwelling on violence or scandal.
So absurd that people find it laughable.
Earning a large amount of money for the people involved.
Extremely angry, often visibly so.
Calm by nature, rarely ruffled by worry or anger.

senses.definition: Thinking straight and aware of one's surroundings, often for a short spell between bouts of confusion.
Giving off light, or letting light pass through; bright or see-through.

mnemonics: Lucid comes from Latin lucere, to shine: a lucid explanation lets light into a murky subject.

senses.definition: Glowing with its own soft light, so that it stands out against the dark.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Giving off a gentle, glowing light.

examples.text: The luminous dial of the antique watch was visible even in total darkness.
A luminous crescent moon hung above the dark outline of the mountain range.
The exit signs are coated with luminous paint so people can find the doors during a blackout.
The deep sea creature had luminous organs that pulsed in the black water far below the surface.

distractors.lemma: Taking up a lot of space, or made of a large amount of material.
Stirring a feeling that something sacred or divine is present.
Giving a sign that trouble or danger is on its way.
Mournful and gloomy in a heavy, exaggerated way.
So costly or destructive that it brings about collapse or bankruptcy.

senses.definition: Very clear and inspiring, as if lit from within; used of writing, art or performances.

mnemonics: Luminous comes from Latin lumen, light, the same root as illuminate: something luminous gives off light.

senses.definition: Big-hearted enough to forgive insults and to treat a beaten or weaker opponent with generosity.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Willing to forgive and be generous, even toward people who opposed you.

examples.text: It was a magnanimous gesture to forgive his old rival and offer him a partnership.
She was magnanimous in victory, praising the hard work of the opponents she had just beaten.
Rather than gloat over the result, the winner gave a magnanimous speech thanking her opponent's supporters and promising to serve them too.
Showing a magnanimous spirit, he overlooked the insults and welcomed his critics into his home.

distractors.lemma: Backed by every single member, with not one voice against.
Too timid to take a stand or face danger.
Commanding and authoritative, like someone used to giving orders.
Grand and splendid, impressive in size or beauty.
Lively and full of energy, especially in speech or movement.

mnemonics: Magnanimous joins Latin magnus, great, and animus, spirit: a great-spirited person rises above grudges.

senses.definition: Pretend to be sick or hurt, or exaggerate an illness, in order to get out of work or duty.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To fake being sick so you can skip work or school.

examples.text: Suspecting that the employee was trying to malinger, the manager asked for a doctor's note.
Army doctors were told to watch for recruits who might malinger by faking back pain before long marches.
Feigning a severe cough is a common tactic for those who wish to malinger.
Video showed the worker lifting heavy boxes at home, proof that he chose to malinger rather than return to his job after his back healed.

distractors.lemma: Stay on somewhere after the reason for being there has passed.
Say harmful, untrue things about someone.
Handle a person or animal in a cruel or abusive way.
Stop working the way it was built to, as a machine might.
Circulate among the guests at a party, chatting briefly with each.

mnemonics: Malinger comes from French malingre, sickly: a malingerer acts sickly to dodge work.

senses.definition: Open to being shaped or changed by others; used of people, beliefs or plans that give way under pressure.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Easy for other people to shape or sway.

examples.text: Young children often have malleable minds that absorb both good and bad influences easily.
The senator proved malleable under pressure, changing his vote after a single meeting with lobbyists.
An inexperienced intern is often malleable and eager to adopt whatever approach the boss prefers.
Public opinion can be surprisingly malleable during a well-funded media campaign.

distractors.lemma: Wanting bad things to happen to others.
Awkward and clumsy, in actions or in dealing with people.
Giving off a nasty smell.
Strong or real enough to be felt or touched.
Unhappy with the way things are and inclined to complain or rebel.

senses.definition: Able to be beaten flat or worked into a shape without breaking apart, as gold and copper are.

mnemonics: Malleable comes from Latin malleus, hammer: a malleable metal, or a malleable mind, can be hammered into a new shape.

senses.definition: Tearful and gushing with sentiment, often feeling sorry for oneself, as some people get after too much drink.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Teary and sentimental in an overdone way, often after too much to drink.

examples.text: After his third glass of wine, Uncle Ray grew maudlin and began tearfully recalling every dog he had ever owned.
The film's maudlin ending, with swelling violins and a deathbed reunion, drew sighs rather than tears from the audience.
His maudlin wedding toast, full of sobbing apologies to people who had long since forgiven him, made the guests shift in their seats.
She kept her retirement speech short and light, determined not to give a maudlin farewell.

distractors.lemma: Biting and sarcastic, used of humor or criticism.
Ordinary and everyday, with nothing exciting about it.
Fascinated by grim things such as dying and decay, more than seems normal.
Mixed up and confused, in thought or in arrangement.
Close to death, or about to come to an end.

mnemonics: Maudlin comes from Magdalene, once pronounced maudlin, because Mary Magdalene was often painted weeping.

senses.definition: Inclined to tell lies; regularly dishonest in what one says.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Lying often, so that what you say cannot be trusted.

examples.text: The mendacious witness was discredited when the defense played security footage that contradicted every detail of his story.
Her mendacious claims about a law degree unraveled when the university said it had no record of her.
Historians found that the diplomat's mendacious letters home described victories that had never happened.
We could not trust the mendacious report, which hid the factory's safety failures behind invented inspection results.

distractors.lemma: Boldly daring, ready to take risks others would avoid.
Getting by on charity, as a beggar or certain religious orders do.
Flashy and eye-catching, yet cheap or hollow once you look closely.
Threatening harm, or seeming likely to cause it.
Holding on firmly and refusing to give up.

senses.definition: Intentionally untrue.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Deliberately false and deceptive.

examples.text: The article contained several mendacious statements designed to mislead investors.
A mendacious rumor circulated through the village before the election.
The contract was voided due to mendacious clauses hidden in the fine print.
Detectives uncovered a mendacious scheme to defraud the insurance company.
A mendacious statement

distractors.lemma: Requiring immediate attention from emergency personnel.
Marked by an absence of color or pigment.
Showing a lack of basic manners and courtesy.
Belonging to a bygone era of classical philosophy.
Exhibiting excessive pride in one's achievements.

mnemonics: Mendacious comes from Latin mendax, lying. Picture a mendacious person whose stories always need mending.

senses.definition: Quick to swing from one mood, opinion or plan to another without warning.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Switching feelings or plans quickly, so people can never guess what comes next.

examples.text: Her mercurial boss could praise a report in the morning and tear it apart by lunch.
The singer's mercurial temper meant an interview could turn from warm to hostile with a single question.
Investors grew wary of the mercurial founder, who reversed the company's strategy three times in one year.
Spring weather in the mountains is mercurial, with sunshine giving way to hail in a matter of minutes.

distractors.lemma: Working only for money, with little concern for anything else.
Showing kindness and forgiveness to someone you could punish.
Having to do with buying, selling and the work of merchants.
Having to do with physical things rather than the mind or spirit.
Having to do with war, soldiers or fighting.

senses.definition: Made with, containing or caused by the metal mercury.
Lively, quick and clever, as the messenger god Mercury was said to be.

mnemonics: Mercurial comes from Mercury, the swift messenger god, and the metal named after him, which slides and splits apart unpredictably.

senses.definition: Taking great care to get every small detail exactly right.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Doing something with extreme attention to every little detail.

examples.text: The artisan was meticulous in his restoration of the old manuscript, matching each faded letter by hand.
Her meticulous research ensured that every historical fact in the novel was correct.
We admired the meticulous craftsmanship of the antique cabinet, where not a single joint showed a gap.
A meticulous editor, she checked every date, name and comma before the book went to print.

distractors.lemma: Always poking into matters that are none of one's concern.
Having to do with rhythm and meter in poetry.
Shaking slightly, often from fear or nerves.
So remarkable that it seems to have no natural explanation.
Worthy of honor, as a brave act or long record of service can be.

mnemonics: Meticulous comes from Latin metus, fear: a meticulous worker is almost afraid of making even one small mistake.

senses.definition: Reduce the harm, force or seriousness of something bad, without removing it entirely.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To soften the damage that something bad can do.

examples.text: The city planted trees along the highway to mitigate the noise from traffic.
New safety rules were introduced to mitigate the risks of factory work.
She took medicine to mitigate the symptoms of her seasonal allergies.
Diplomats worked for weeks to mitigate the tensions between the two nations.

distractors.lemma: Act as a strong force against an outcome, as evidence can against a verdict.
Take a dispute to court, or argue a case there.
Move from one region to another, often with the seasons.
Set something in motion, especially trouble or unrest.
Damage a body or object badly by cutting off or destroying parts.

senses.definition: Make a wrong or crime seem less serious, as facts offered in someone's defense can.

mnemonics: Mitigate comes from Latin mitis, mild: to mitigate damage is to make it milder.

senses.definition: Calm someone's anger or ease their worry, whether with an apology, kind words or a small concession.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To calm down someone who is angry or upset, for example with an apology or a kind word.

examples.text: The airline handed out meal vouchers to mollify passengers who had waited six hours at the gate.
A quick, sincere apology was enough to mollify the neighbor whose fence our dog had dug under.
Nothing the mayor said could mollify the crowd, which kept shouting until he left the stage.
He brought flowers home to mollify his wife after forgetting their anniversary.

distractors.lemma: Treat someone too gently and protect them too much.
Change something partly, without altering it completely.
Cancel the force of something, so it no longer counts.
Shame someone so badly that they want to disappear.

senses.definition: Make something softer or less rigid.
Make a demand, opinion or statement milder and easier to accept.

mnemonics: Mollify comes from Latin mollis, soft: you mollify an angry person by softening their mood.

senses.definition: In a dark, sulky mood, keeping to oneself and refusing to be cheered.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Being gloomy, sullen, and in a bad mood.

examples.text: He sat in the corner with a morose expression, refusing to join the celebration.
The week of rain seemed to put the whole household into a morose state of mind.
Her usually cheerful personality turned morose after the disappointing news, and she barely spoke for days.
The novel's hero is a morose detective who rarely speaks to anyone and never smiles.

distractors.lemma: Wordy, saying in twenty words what could be said in five.
Pointless and unneeded, adding nothing of value.
Spoiling for a fight, or eager for war.
Pompously grand, aiming to impress more than it can deliver.
Full of tiny holes that let liquid or air pass through.

mnemonics: Morose comes from Latin morosus, peevish or hard to please: a morose person sulks and will not be cheered.

senses.definition: Part of the routine of daily life, and so dull rather than remarkable.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Ordinary and a bit dull, like the everyday chores everyone has to do.

examples.text: Doing the laundry and washing dishes are mundane tasks that fill up her weekends.
He sought to escape his mundane routine by planning an adventurous trip abroad.
Even famous artists must deal with mundane paperwork like paying taxes.
After months of exciting fieldwork, she dreaded the mundane job of typing her notes into a spreadsheet.

distractors.lemma: Smooth, polished and at ease in social settings.
Closely tied to the topic being discussed.
Showing kindness and a wish to spare others from suffering.
Foolish and without any real sense or content.
In the habit of telling lies.

senses.definition: Relating to this world and its practical affairs rather than to spiritual or heavenly things.

mnemonics: Mundane comes from Latin mundus, world: mundane things belong to the ordinary everyday world.

senses.definition: Giving money or gifts far more freely and lavishly than most people would.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Very generous, especially with large gifts of money.

examples.text: Thanks to a munificent donation from a former student, the college now offers free tuition to every nursing student.
Her munificent gift allowed the museum to buy a collection of rare manuscripts.
The host was munificent, paying for every guest's flight and hotel during the week-long wedding.
Workers expected a small bonus, so the owner's munificent payout of a full month's salary stunned them.

distractors.lemma: Grand and impressive in size, beauty or style.
Bringing harm or evil on others.
Run by or belonging to the local council of a town.
Expert enough at a skill to do it smoothly.
Missing some part or quality that is needed.

mnemonics: Munificent comes from Latin munus, gift, and facere, to make: a munificent person makes many gifts.

senses.definition: An extreme state of adversity; the lowest point of anything.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: The absolute lowest point of a difficult situation.

examples.text: Sleeping in his car after losing both his job and his apartment, he felt he had reached the nadir of his life.
That bitter argument, when neither spoke for a year, was the nadir of their long friendship.
The stock hit its nadir in March, at a tenth of its peak value, before slowly recovering.
After hitting the nadir of his career, he slowly began to rebuild.

distractors.lemma: A nymph in Greek myth who lived in a river, spring or lake.
Someone who has grown rich and powerful, especially one who shows it off.
A point where lines, branches or pathways meet.
The shiny, rainbow-colored layer that lines some shells.

senses.definition: The point below the observer that is directly opposite the zenith on the imaginary sphere against which celestial bodies appear to be projected.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: The point in the sky directly beneath where you are standing.

examples.text: The telescope was pointed straight down toward the nadir.
Astronomy students calculated the exact nadir for their nighttime observations.
The plumb line pointed directly at the local nadir.
Celestial coordinates require charting both the zenith and the nadir.

distractors.lemma: The highest point in the celestial sphere.
A device used to measure atmospheric pressure.
The center point of a planetary orbit.
A bright constellation visible in winter.
The angle of inclination of a star.

mnemonics: Nadir comes from Arabic nazir, opposite: the nadir is the point opposite the zenith, the very bottom.

senses.definition: In the earliest stage of existence or growth, and not yet fully formed.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: New and only starting to grow or take shape.

examples.text: The country's nascent democracy, only two years old, still lacked a working court system.
Investors like to back nascent companies early, before their first product has even launched.
A nascent feeling of doubt began to grow in his mind as the salesman kept talking.
The town's nascent music scene consists of three bands and one small club that opened last spring.

distractors.lemma: Relating to the nose.
Not knowing; without knowledge or awareness.
Next door to, or touching, something else.
Inactive or at rest for the time being.
Going on and on with no letup.

mnemonics: Nascent comes from Latin nasci, to be born, the root of natal and renaissance: a nascent thing has just been born.

senses.definition: Lacking definite form or limits.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Vague and hazy, with no clear shape, edges or details.

examples.text: The candidate's plan to fix the economy stayed nebulous; he never named a single policy or its cost.
Her memory of the accident is nebulous, just a blur of headlights and noise.
The contract's nebulous wording about reasonable delays led to a long fight over who was at fault.
The smoke formed nebulous wisps in the cold air.

distractors.lemma: Made up of a large number of things or people.
So remarkable it seems to belong in a legend.
Able to poison or injure living things.
Trembling a little, as from fear or weakness.
Working hard and with steady care.

senses.definition: Relating to or resembling a cloud of gas and dust in outer space.

mnemonics: Nebulous comes from Latin nebula, mist: a nebulous idea is misty, with no clear outline.

senses.definition: Thoroughly evil, often in a way that also breaks the law.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Very bad and wicked, like a villain's plan.

examples.text: The hackers had a nefarious plan: lock the hospital's records and demand a ransom to release them.
She uncovered a nefarious scheme to steal retirees' savings through a fake charity.
The detective vowed to stop the gang's nefarious plot to poison the city's water supply.
Cartoon villains twirl their mustaches while explaining their nefarious plans to the captured hero.

distractors.lemma: Made up of many different kinds or parts.
Unstable and at risk of falling or failing.
Enjoyed secondhand, by watching or hearing about someone else's experience.
Happiest when surrounded by other people.
So funny that it makes people laugh hard.

mnemonics: Nefarious comes from Latin nefas, a crime against divine law (ne-, not, plus fas, what is right).

senses.definition: Someone who has only just started an activity or field and lacks experience in it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A beginner who has just started something new.

examples.text: As a neophyte at the climbing gym, she spent her first week learning how to tie knots and fall safely.
The chess club pairs each neophyte with an experienced player who explains the basic openings.
Wine experts sometimes forget that a neophyte cannot yet tell a merlot from a cabernet.
Even after a year in office, the senator was still seen as a neophyte who did not know how deals got made.

distractors.lemma: A word that someone has recently made up.
An abnormal growth of tissue, such as a tumor.
A plant that grows on another plant for support but takes no food from it.
The habit of giving jobs or favors to one's own relatives.

senses.definition: A new convert being taught the principles of Christianity by a catechist.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A person newly converted to Christianity who is receiving religious instruction.

examples.text: The bishop spent hours answering the theological questions of each eager neophyte.
During the ceremony, the neophyte made a public profession of faith before the congregation.
Catechists guided every neophyte through the foundational doctrines of the church.
The ancient text details the specific rites performed for a neophyte before baptism.

distractors.lemma: An ordained priest responsible for maintaining parish records and archives.
A wandering philosopher who questions traditional religious dogmas.
A secular musician hired to perform hymns during Sunday services.
A monastery librarian tasked with translating sacred manuscripts into Latin.

senses.definition: A plant that is found in an area where it had not been recorded previously.

mnemonics: Neophyte comes from Greek neos, new, and phytos, planted: a neophyte is newly planted in a field.

senses.definition: Hardened against every appeal, so that neither reason nor sympathy can soften one's stand.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Stubborn and hard-hearted, refusing to give in or change.

examples.text: Despite tearful pleas from the family, the obdurate landlord refused to delay the eviction by even a day.
She tried every argument she could think of, but her father remained obdurate about selling the farm.
The committee's obdurate opposition to any change kept the outdated rules in place for decades.
The judge was struck by how obdurate the defendant remained, showing no remorse even as the victims spoke.

distractors.lemma: Left behind by newer things and no longer used.
Required by a rule, law or custom.
Known to few people, or hard to make out.
Possible to put up with or bear.

senses.definition: Persisting in wrongdoing and showing no regret for it.

mnemonics: Obdurate comes from Latin obdurare, to harden, from durus, hard: an obdurate heart has hardened and will not bend.

senses.definition: Make something harder to understand or see clearly, often on purpose.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To make something confusing on purpose so that people cannot follow it.

examples.text: When asked about the missing funds, the treasurer tried to obfuscate the problem with a flood of acronyms and charts.
The insurance policy seemed written to obfuscate what was covered, burying every exclusion in footnotes.
A good teacher makes a hard idea clear instead of using jargon to obfuscate it.
Rather than admit the delay, the airline sent a vague notice that seemed meant to obfuscate the real reason.

distractors.lemma: Make something unnecessary by dealing with it in advance.
Barge in with opinions or company that nobody asked for.
Seize someone's goods under official power, as customs officers do with smuggled items.
Choke from having no air to breathe.
Bind someone by law or duty to do something.

mnemonics: Obfuscate comes from Latin fuscus, dark: to obfuscate is to darken a point until no one can see it clearly.

senses.definition: Too eager to obey, agree with or flatter others, in a way that seems servile.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Acting overly obedient and flattering in order to gain approval from powerful people.

examples.text: The obsequious waiter bowed every time the owner passed and laughed loudly at jokes that were not funny.
Surrounded by obsequious courtiers, the monarch rarely heard an honest opinion.
His obsequious praise of the director felt insincere and overly calculated.
She despised the obsequious behavior of colleagues who constantly agreed with every management decision.

distractors.lemma: Failing to notice what is going on nearby.
Loud, unruly and hard to keep in order.
Popping up in every place one looks.
So rude or annoying that people want to avoid you.
Thinking about one thing far more than is healthy or normal.

mnemonics: Obsequious comes from Latin obsequi, to comply, literally to follow after: an obsequious person follows the boss's every wish.

senses.definition: Firmly sticking to one's own way and resisting every attempt at persuasion.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Being extremely stubborn and refusing to change your mind no matter what.

examples.text: My obstinate grandfather refused to wear a hearing aid, no matter how often we had to repeat ourselves.
The toddler turned obstinate at bedtime, planting her feet and shaking her head at every offer of a story.
The mule proved too obstinate to move down the narrow mountain trail.
Even after three doctors told him to rest, the obstinate runner insisted on racing the next day.

distractors.lemma: Part of someone's nature from birth, not learned.
Loaded with fancy carving, gilding or trim.
Relating to pregnancy and the delivery of babies.
Showy in a way meant to draw attention and impress others.

senses.definition: Hard to get rid of, cure or bring under control.

mnemonics: Obstinate comes from Latin obstinare, to persist, a relative of stare, to stand: the obstinate stand their ground and will not budge.

senses.definition: Slow to grasp what is meant or to notice what is obvious, sometimes deliberately.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Slow to understand things, or pretending not to get them.

examples.text: He was being deliberately obtuse, pretending not to understand that 'we should talk later' meant 'please leave now.'
Even the most obtuse reader will notice that every villain in the novel wears green.
I hinted three times that the party was a surprise, but my obtuse brother still asked her what time it started.
Is the committee really so obtuse that it cannot see why nobody applies for these jobs?

distractors.lemma: So complex or specialized that few people can follow it.
So prominent that it gets in the way or annoys.
So plentiful that it overflows, like tears or thanks that keep coming.
Scattered widely rather than gathered in one place.

senses.definition: Describing an angle wider than a right angle but narrower than a straight line.
Of a leaf or other plant part, blunt or rounded at the tip.

mnemonics: Obtuse comes from Latin obtusus, blunted: an obtuse mind is dull rather than sharp, like an angle too wide to come to a point.

senses.definition: Intrusive in a meddling or offensive manner.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Being overly eager to give unwanted help or advice in an annoying way.

examples.text: The officious security guard demanded to inspect my identification three times.
We grew tired of the hotel manager and his officious interference in our vacation.
An officious clerk made us redo every form in blue ink, though no rule required it.
She resented her neighbor's officious advice on how to prune her rose bushes.

distractors.lemma: Approved by, or acting on behalf of, a government or other authority.
Working well enough to bring about the result that was wanted.
Fawning, and keen to obey or flatter people with power.
Joking about a serious matter at a moment when humor is out of place.
Seeming to promise that things will turn out well.

mnemonics: Officious comes from Latin officium, "duty", the root of office: an officious person treats every matter as their duty to manage.

senses.definition: Heavy and tiring to carry out, because it demands a lot of effort, cost or responsibility.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Hard and tiring to do, like a heavy load you have to carry.

examples.text: The monarch imposed onerous taxes on the peasantry to fund the foreign war.
Managing the large estate alone proved to be an onerous task for the young heir.
The loan came with onerous terms: twenty percent interest and a penalty for paying early.
The paperwork required by the new rules became too onerous for the small bakery to handle.
My duties weren't onerous at all; I only had to greet the guests at the door.

distractors.lemma: Giving off a smell, often a strong one.
Containing a mistake or resting on a false belief.
Amounting to a large count of separate things.
Having to do with dreams or the act of dreaming.
Ready to give more money, time or help than is expected.

mnemonics: Onerous comes from Latin onus, "burden", the same onus as in "the onus is on you".

senses.definition: Difficult to understand or see into, because the meaning or the workings are hidden.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: So unclear or closed off that people cannot tell what it means or how it works.

examples.text: The contract's opaque language left even our lawyer unsure what we had agreed to.
Critics said the charity's budget was opaque, with millions of dollars listed only under vague headings.
His reasons for quitting remained opaque; he simply cleared his desk and left without a word.
The philosopher's prose is so opaque that students read each paragraph three times before it makes sense.

distractors.lemma: Showing great wealth through rich, costly furnishings or goods.
Happening at a convenient or well-chosen time.
Being the best choice available under the conditions.
Having to do with eyes, sight or the way light behaves.
Belonging to opera, or as dramatic and overblown as an opera.

senses.definition: Blocking light so that nothing can be seen through it.

mnemonics: Opaque comes from Latin opacus, "shaded": an opaque explanation leaves its meaning in the shade.

senses.definition: Scornful public blame heaped on a person or group for behavior seen as disgraceful.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A harsh wave of public shame and criticism directed at someone.

examples.text: The corrupt politician faced severe opprobrium after the financial scandal broke.
The referee faced the opprobrium of the entire stadium after his call cost the home team the final.
The dictator earned international opprobrium for his human rights abuses.
When diners learned the chef had been serving reheated frozen meals as 'made fresh daily', the opprobrium online forced the restaurant to close.

distractors.lemma: Harsh treatment of a group by those in control, denying them fair rights.
A state of confused thinking and wild excitement, often caused by fever or illness.
A steady condition where competing pressures cancel out and nothing shifts.
A grand old shop where you could buy almost anything under one roof.
An agreed pause on an activity for a set period of time.

senses.definition: A state of extreme dishonor.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A deep and lasting sense of shame or humiliation.

examples.text: He lived in deep opprobrium following his conviction for fraud.
The fallen general retreated into solitude to escape public opprobrium.
Centuries later, the tyrant's name is still synonymous with absolute opprobrium.
She preferred exile to living under the heavy burden of local opprobrium.
The name was a by-word of scorn and opprobrium throughout the city

distractors.lemma: A condition of supreme happiness and satisfaction.
The legal procedure for claiming lost property.
An elevated status granted by academic achievement.
A temporary leave of absence from duties.
The ceremonial blessing of a new building.

mnemonics: Opprobrium comes from Latin probrum, "a shameful act": opprobrium is the scorn heaped on someone who commits one.

senses.definition: Intended to attract notice and impress others.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Showing off in a flashy way to make people notice and admire you.

examples.text: The billionaire threw an ostentatious party featuring exotic animals and ice sculptures.
Rather than an ostentatious mansion, the founder bought a modest bungalow and drove a ten-year-old car.
His ostentatious display of wealth alienated his more modest friends.
The palace was decorated in an ostentatious style with gold leaf on every surface.
She arrived at the small country wedding in an ostentatious sable coat and a diamond tiara.

distractors.lemma: Presented as the real reason or fact, though it may not be.
Prone to provoke quarrels and heated debate.
Pushing one side of a disputed question instead of treating it fairly.
Consisting of bone, or hard and bony in texture.
Taking great care to do every task properly and fully.

mnemonics: Ostentatious comes from Latin ostentare, "to keep showing": an ostentatious person keeps showing off what they own.

senses.definition: Make something bad seem or feel less severe without dealing with what causes it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To make a problem, mistake, or bad situation seem less severe than it is.

examples.text: The spokesperson tried to palliate the company's financial losses with optimistic projections.
No amount of clever rhetoric can palliate the gravity of their offense.
He attempted to palliate his tardiness by blaming the sudden transit strike.
The report tried to palliate the factory's safety failures by calling them minor paperwork lapses.

distractors.lemma: Examine a part of the body by pressing and feeling it with the hands.
Carry pollen to a flower so that it can make seeds.
Gather pages or pieces of information and put them in order.
Lose its charm after being enjoyed too often.
Fill an area with people who come to live there.

senses.definition: Ease the symptoms of an illness, such as pain, without curing it.

mnemonics: Palliate comes from Latin pallium, "cloak": to palliate a fault is to throw a cloak over it so it looks less bad.

senses.definition: A single remedy believed to cure every illness or to solve every problem.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: One cure or fix that is supposed to solve all problems at once.

examples.text: Many medieval scholars spent their lives searching for a true panacea that could cure any ailment known to humanity.
The ambitious new tax policy was touted by politicians as a panacea for the struggling national economy.
We must accept that there is no simple panacea for the complex social issues facing our modern society.
Exercise helps with many ailments, but it is not a panacea; some conditions still need medicine.

distractors.lemma: The organ near the stomach whose cells release insulin and enzymes that break down food.
A wide view that takes in a whole landscape in every direction.
An outbreak of disease that spreads across many countries at once.
A pill with no active drug in it, given for its effect on the mind.
The group of the most admired people in a field.

mnemonics: Panacea comes from Greek pan, "all", and akos, "cure": a panacea is a cure for all.

senses.definition: An ideal instance; a perfect embodiment of a concept.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Someone or something so excellent that others treat it as the perfect example.

examples.text: Never late, never rude and always prepared, she was a paragon of professionalism in a chaotic office.
The newly restored cathedral stands as a paragon of Gothic architecture in the heart of the city.
He saw his grandfather, who returned every lost wallet he ever found, as a paragon of honesty.
The restaurant was hailed as a paragon of good service, where waiters remembered every regular's order.

distractors.lemma: A claim that sounds impossible or self-defeating but may hold up on closer thought.
A plane figure, like a triangle or hexagon, whose edges are all straight.
A secret lover of someone who is married to another person.
A block of writing that deals with one point and begins on a new line.
A waxy substance made from petroleum and used in candles.

mnemonics: Paragon comes from Italian paragone, a touchstone used to test gold: a paragon is the standard others are tested against.

senses.definition: Extreme care in spending money; reluctance to spend money unnecessarily.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Being very careful with money and refusing to spend it unless totally necessary.

examples.text: His legendary parsimony meant that he reused even the smallest scraps of wrapping paper.
The corporate office enforced strict parsimony regarding travel expenses and office supplies.
Despite his great wealth, a streak of parsimony prevented him from ever tipping generously.
Her parsimony allowed her to save enough money to buy a house by age twenty-five.

distractors.lemma: Harsh, bitter anger between people who disagree.
Marriage, especially when seen as a formal or religious bond.
Wealth or traditions handed down from a father or earlier forebears.
A comic imitation that mocks the style of a writer, artist or genre.
The home where a parish clergyman lives, owned by his church.

senses.definition: The preference, in science or argument, for the simplest explanation that accounts for the facts.

mnemonics: Parsimony comes from Latin parcere, "to spare": a person known for parsimony spares every coin.

senses.definition: An insufficient quantity or number.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A very small amount of something when more is needed.

examples.text: The severe drought resulted in a concerning paucity of fresh water for the local livestock.
Investigators noted a frustrating paucity of physical evidence at the crime scene.
Due to the paucity of applicants, the university extended the deadline for the scholarship.
The historian lamented the paucity of reliable written records from that specific century.

distractors.lemma: A person with almost no money or possessions.
Nerve or boldness, especially the kind that shocks other people.
Honesty in what a person says, or the accuracy of a claim.
The largest amount that a container or system can hold.
A round, heavy stomach that bulges over the belt.

mnemonics: Paucity comes from Latin paucus, "few": a paucity of anything means there are too few of them.

senses.definition: Marked by a narrow focus on, or display of, learning, especially its trivial aspects.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Being overly focused on minor rules, tiny details, or showing off academic knowledge.

examples.text: The professor delivered a pedantic lecture that focused entirely on comma placements rather than the themes.
He corrected his friends' grammar during a casual chat, earning a reputation for being pedantic.
Her pedantic approach to grading meant that even the slightest formatting error lost points.
Instead of enjoying the film, he made pedantic notes about historical inaccuracies in the costumes.

distractors.lemma: Having to do with the health care of babies and children.
Having to do with teaching or the methods used to teach.
Plain and ordinary, with no spark of imagination.
Drooping and heavy, so that it sways when moved.

mnemonics: Pedantic comes from pedant, which came into English through French from Italian pedante, a schoolmaster: a pedantic person corrects everyone like a fussy teacher.

senses.definition: An enduring taste for something, or a natural pull toward doing it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A strong liking for something that you keep coming back to.

examples.text: She has a well-known penchant for gothic literature and dark mystery novels.
During his travels, he developed a strong penchant for spicy street food.
The artist had a penchant for using vibrant blues and greens in every canvas.
His penchant for telling elaborate jokes made him popular at social gatherings.

distractors.lemma: An ornament worn dangling on a chain or cord at the throat.
A narrow triangular flag, such as one flown to honor a sports champion.
Hardship a person takes on willingly to make up for a wrong they did.
Regular payments made to someone after they retire from work.
A short phrase sung or shouted over and over by a group.

mnemonics: Penchant comes from French pencher, "to lean": a penchant is a natural leaning toward something.

senses.definition: A state of extreme poverty or destitution.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A condition of extreme poverty where someone lacks basic necessities.

examples.text: The prolonged economic depression plunged many families into deep penury.
He spent his youth in penury before finding success as an author.
After the factory closed, the family lived in such penury that they burned old furniture for heat.
The painter died in penury, and only years later did his canvases sell for millions.

distractors.lemma: The crime of giving testimony one knows to be false after swearing to tell the truth.
A hardship a person takes on willingly to show regret for having done wrong.
The pale fringe of half-shadow that surrounds the darkest part of a shadow.
A lasting fondness or taste for a particular thing or activity.
A long, tapering flag, often flown on a ship or awarded to a winning team.

mnemonics: Penury sounds like penniless, meaning having no money at all.

senses.definition: Given to breaking faith with those who depend on one's loyalty.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Likely to turn on the friends or partners who trusted you.

examples.text: The perfidious ally signed the peace treaty in the morning and opened the city gates to the enemy that night.
She could not forgive her perfidious business partner, who had secretly sold their client list to a rival.
History remembers the general as perfidious because he switched sides in the middle of the battle.
Tell a perfidious friend your secret, and you will soon hear it repeated all over the office.

distractors.lemma: Carried out as a routine duty, with little care or interest.
Deliberately contrary, choosing the opposite of what is sensible or wanted.
Fussy about neatness and detail, and quick to notice any small flaw.
Unfair in a way that stirs up envy or bad feeling, as when one person is singled out.

mnemonics: Perfidious holds fid, from Latin fides (faith), as in fidelity; the per- turns it around, so a perfidious person breaks faith.

senses.definition: Hasty and without attention to detail; not thorough.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Done quickly and carelessly without paying attention to important details.

examples.text: The inspector gave the machinery a perfunctory glance before signing off.
She offered a perfunctory apology and rushed out of the room.
His perfunctory review of the manuscript missed several major errors.
The doctor's perfunctory checkup lasted two minutes, and she never asked about his symptoms.

distractors.lemma: Commanding in a way that leaves no room for questions or refusal.
Having stopped operating or existing, as a closed company or a dead program.
Bearing closely on the question at hand, and so worth raising.
Going on without end, or repeated so often that it seems never to stop.

senses.definition: Done or produced as a formality only.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Done simply as a routine duty or formality without real care.

examples.text: He gave a perfunctory nod to the audience as he took the stage.
The handshake between the rivals was entirely perfunctory.
She completed the mandatory paperwork with a perfunctory wave of her hand.
Their polite greetings were merely perfunctory gestures.

distractors.lemma: Pertaining to the function of mechanical parts.
Carried out with deep emotional involvement.
Created through a complex artistic process.
Designed to provoke a strong public reaction.
Involving a high degree of personal risk.

mnemonics: Perfunctory comes from Latin perfungi, to get through a duty: a perfunctory job is done just to be finished with it.

senses.definition: Causing great harm that spreads quietly, so it may go unnoticed until late.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Very harmful, often in a slow way that is easy to miss.

examples.text: Lead in old water pipes is pernicious because the damage builds up quietly over many years.
The pernicious idea that girls are bad at math kept many talented students out of science classes.
Gossip had a pernicious effect on the team, slowly turning colleagues against one another.
Pollution has a pernicious effect on marine life long before anyone sees dead fish on the beach.

distractors.lemma: Hard to satisfy because of an endless focus on trivial things.
Developing adult skills or tastes at an unusually young age.
Allowing more freedom than is usual or expected.
Lasting for a long time or coming back year after year.

mnemonics: Pernicious comes from Latin pernicies, ruin, built on nex, violent death, the same root found in internecine.

senses.definition: Acutely insightful and wise.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Quick to see what is really going on, even when others miss it.

examples.text: The perspicacious investor sold her shares months before the market crash that surprised everyone else.
She was far too perspicacious to be fooled by such a flimsy argument.
A perspicacious teacher can tell at a glance which student has not done the reading.
His perspicacious review pointed out the flaw in the study that the authors themselves had missed.

distractors.lemma: Written or spoken so plainly that the meaning is easy to grasp.
Refusing to let go of a goal or belief, even after repeated setbacks.
Looking reasonable at first glance while being wrong underneath.
Always spoiling for a quarrel or a fight.

mnemonics: Perspicacious comes from Latin perspicere, to see through, the same root as perspective: a perspicacious person sees through to the truth.

senses.definition: Reaching into every corner of a place, group or system, so that little is left untouched.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Found everywhere, so you cannot get away from it.

examples.text: The pervasive smell of smoke clung to the curtains, the carpet and every coat in the closet.
Corruption was so pervasive that even the clerks expected a bribe to stamp a form.
Smartphones have become pervasive, and it is hard to find a train passenger without one.
